The results from the world's largest payments processor underscore a robust US economy in the face of persistent inflationary pressures as consumers continue spending, underpinned by a strong labor market and wage growth. "Growth across consumer spend bands remained relatively consistent with prior quarters, with the highest spend band continuing to grow the fastest. We did not see signs of the lower spend consumer weakening in our volumes," Visa finance chief Chris Suh said in a post-earnings call. Payments volume, a gauge of consumer and business spending on Visa's network, jumped 9% in the reported quarter on a constant-dollar basis, while processed transactions rose 10%. Visa's extensive digital payments network, which spans more than 200 countries and territories, positions it to better endure economic downturns as billions of people globally rely on the card network for everyday spending and other purchases. CLIENT INCENTIVES, PROFIT FORECAST IN FOCUS Client incentives jumped 21% to $5.1 billion in the quarter from the prior year, largely driven by new deals that were signed during the July to September period and early in the fourth quarter. "The one thing to nitpick is client incentives, which were above expectations," Seaport analyst Jeff Cantwell said, adding the development likely impacted Visa's fiscal 2027 forecasts. Suh told analysts incentives growth would step up in fiscal 2027 as Visa is expecting around 25% of its payments volumes to be renewed, including with several large clients. That compares with 20% in fiscal 2026. The company anticipates fiscal 2027 profit per share growth between a low-double-digit and low-teens percentage, while net revenue growth is expected to be in the low-double-digit percentage. "While some may be underwhelmed by the EPS guide, we think it likely reflects... (the management's) decision to keep investing in long-term strategic initiatives to extend the durability of top-line growth," KBW analysts led by Sanjay Sakhrani said. Visa's shares fell about 1.4% in extended trading. The stock has gained 14.6% this year through the last close. On an adjusted basis, it earned $3.48 per share in the three months ended September 30, beating an expectation of $3.44 per share, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. CROSS-BORDER STRENGTH Cross-border volumes excluding intra-Europe, a measure of international travel demand, were a bright spot as they jumped 14% in the quarter on a constant-dollar basis. "It is reflective of strong consumer sentiment, strong demand for travel experiences, and the fact that e-commerce has also just expanded," Suh said. Suh told Reuters travel in and out of the Middle East was also coming back closer to normal levels after being suppressed due to the Iran conflict. The FIFA World Cup, which ran from June 11 to July 19, has also helped boost activity across Visa's network as it brought many visitors to the United States. "XB (cross-border) showed a nice step-up in growth sequentially, and that was one area we were watching for signs of potential weakness going into earnings," Seaport's Cantwell said. Net revenue jumped 13% to $12.1 billion in the quarter. For fiscal year 2026, Visa hauled record net revenue of $46 billion. Rival Mastercard (MA.N) is set to report quarterly earnings later this week.

item.title: Expand Energy tops estimates as output rises; EQT earnings decline
item.description: Top US natural gas producer Expand Energy surpassed Wall Street expectations for third-quarter profit on Tuesday, boosted by higher natural gas output.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Top US natural gas producer Expand Energy (EXE.O) surpassed Wall Street expectations for third-quarter profit on Tuesday, boosted by higher natural gas output. U.S. natural gas producers are benefiting from rising demand from electric utilities to power data centers and from increasing liquefied natural gas exports, even as abundant supply has kept prices under pressure. U.S. natural gas consumption is expected to hit record highs, also driven by power demand from AI data centers. For the quarter ended September 30, Expand's natural gas production averaged about 7.54 billion cubic feet equivalent per day, up from about 7.33 Bcfe/d a year ago. Expand Energy is the largest independent natural gas producer in the U.S., based on net daily production, and operates mainly in Appalachia and the Haynesville. It posted an adjusted profit of $1.46 per share for the quarter, compared with analysts' average estimate of $1.27 per share, according to data compiled by LSEG. EQT POSTS LOWER PROFIT AS PRODUCTION WEIGHS Rival EQT (EQT.N) , which earlier this week agreed to [USN:L3N46C0NK TEXT:"buy Range Resources"] (RRC.N) in a $13 billion all-stock deal, posted lower third-quarter profit on Tuesday as its production fell for the quarter. EQT's average realized price for natural gas production for the quarter fell about 1.5% to $2.72 per thousand cubic feet equivalent from a year ago, driven by weakness in US natural gas futures . The company aims to retake its spot as the largest US natgas producer with the Range deal. EQT expects the combined company to have net production of more than 9 bcfe/d. Meanwhile, Expand on Tuesday narrowed its annual production forecast to 7.45-7.55 bcfe/d, from 7.4-7.6 bcfe/d, previously. Net income attributable to EQT fell about 17% to $279 million during the quarter. But its adjusted profit of 42 cents per share still managed to exceed analysts' expectations of 39 cents per share. Shares of Expand rose 1.5% in extended trading, while EQT fell 1.1%.

item.title: Live: Israel votes in pivotal election as Netanyahu faces main rival Eisenkot
item.description: Israel's election ended in an apparent deadlock, exit polls by major television networks showed, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot on track for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
item.dc:creator: Estelle Shirbon, Vanessa Balintec, Lioman Lima

item.title: Lazio crush Sassuolo to go top, Roma and Como win late
item.description: Lazio maintained their unbeaten start to the season and moved provisionally top of the Serie A standings with a 6-2 win at Sassuolo on Tuesday, while AS Roma kept pace with a 4-2 victory over Cagliari and Como won 3-1 at Torino.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Lazio maintained their unbeaten start to the season and moved provisionally top of the Serie A standings with a 6-2 win at Sassuolo on Tuesday, while AS Roma kept pace with a 4-2 victory over Cagliari and Como won 3-1 at Torino. Gennaro Gattuso's Lazio side have eight wins from nine games and are on 25 points, three ahead of Inter Milan, who visit bottom club Venezia on Wednesday. Roma are one point further back in third, one point ahead of Como. Lazio, backed by a sizeable away support, roared into a second-minute lead through Kenneth Taylor but the game had barely restarted following a lengthy VAR check when Sassuolo equalised through a Josip Sutalo own-goal. Lazio looked in control with quick goals from Gustav Isaksen and Romano Floriani Mussolini before Sassuolo's hopes of a comeback took a hammering just after the half-hour mark when Kristian Thorstvedt was shown a red card for a foul on Mattia Zaccagni. Sassuolo did, however, pull a goal back two minutes from halftime through Sebastiano Esposito only to see Lazio restore their two-goal advantage in added time before the break when Zaccagni was allowed a free header from Isaksen's cross. Zaccagni spurned a chance to score again shortly after the interval when Simone Cinquegrano's handball gave Lazio a penalty, but the captain's tame spot kick was saved by Stefano Turati. Lazio found a fifth goal with Tijjani Noslin's curled shot from outside the box before a foul by Duje Caleta-Car on Isaksen gave the visitors another penalty, and this time Turati saved from Davide Frattesi. Noslin again made up for Lazio's wastefulness from the spot with another strike from distance to complete the scoring as Gattuso's side continue to look like real title contenders. "We don't have to look at the standings because both I and many of them are not used to it and therefore we have to do things seriously and at a thousand miles per hour," Gattuso said. ROMA AND COMO EARN LATE WINS The Stadio Olimpico was temporarily silenced when Cagliari took the lead in the 10th minute from the penalty spot, with M'Bala Nzola converting after a handball by Niccolo Pisilli. Roma drew level five minutes later with Emanuele Lulli's header from a pinpoint cross by Nahuel Molina and the hosts went ahead in the 21st minute when Lulli turned provider, his cross volleyed to the net by Pisilli. Keeper Pierluigi Gollini was called into action on several occasions in the second half and kept Roma in front until Daniel Maldini netted Cagliari's equaliser nine minutes from time. Roma looked set to slip further behind the leaders until Rodrigo Mora and Donyell Malen both scored in the final five minutes. Che Adams put Torino ahead in the 24th minute, and the hosts were on course to win their fourth successive game until three goals in the last 10 minutes from Jacobo Ramon, Nico Paz and Martin Baturina earned Como an unlikely victory.

item.title: Parents of Alex Pretti slam Trump administration for withholding evidence into his killing
item.description: The parents of Alex Pretti, a US citizen shot and killed by federal immigration agents in Minnesota in January, criticized President Donald Trump's administration on Tuesday for withholding evidence from local prosecutors who are investigating the incident.
item.dc:creator: Julia Harte
item.content:encoded: The parents of Alex Pretti, a US citizen [USN:S0N3WW007 TEXT:"shot and killed by federal immigration agents"] in Minnesota in January, criticized President Donald Trump's administration on Tuesday for withholding evidence from local prosecutors who are investigating the incident. "Our experience with the Department of Justice has left us wondering how Alex will ever get justice," Pretti's father Michael said at a press conference in Minneapolis, the first time the family has spoken publicly since his death. "Do your job and stop shielding Alex's killers," he demanded. The Justice Department said in a statement to Reuters that "communications with family members, if any, come at a later stage of a case, such as indictment, initial appearance, plea, trial, or sentencing. Those communications do not typically occur during an investigation." Pretti, 37, an intensive-care-unit nurse, was killed while participating in protests against the federal immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis, shortly after ICE agents fatally shot another US citizen, Renee Good. Their deaths sparked fierce protests, condemnations from local leaders and calls for accountability. FIGHT OVER EVIDENCE Trump officials swiftly [USN:L1N3YQ04Q TEXT:"defended the Border Patrol agents"] who killed Pretti, claiming he was trying to attack them with a handgun he was carrying legally. But [USN:S0N3WW007 TEXT:"bystander videos showed"] Pretti had a phone in his hand and was trying to help a protester who had been pushed to the ground when agents pinned him down and shot him. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty launched a criminal investigation soon after Pretti’s death. In March, she [USN:L6N40C16O TEXT:"sued the Trump administration"] for access to evidence in the killings of Pretti and Good, as well as the non-lethal shooting of a Venezuelan man by an immigration agent in January. Moriarty [USN:L1N43F0OM TEXT:"said in July"] that the federal government was handing over "voluminous" evidence related to the shootings. When her office examined the material from the Minnesota US Attorney's Office, however, it realized "some information had been withheld," Moriarty said earlier this month in a declaration filed in federal district court in Washington. "Furthermore, it is clear that the federal government has obtained additional material since they last shared information with the State," including material obtained through grand jury processes and other witness statements, Moriarty said in the filing. US prosecutors responded that they were not obligated to release further evidence because Moriarty's office had not yet initiated legal proceedings in the case. "The timing is consistent with how these types of investigations proceed," the DOJ said in its statement. "It has been a miserable year for our family," Pretti's mother Susan said at Tuesday's press conference. "All we want is justice for Alex [and] that the federal government treat us with the dignity and respect that our son deserves."

item.title: Giants won't alter trade deadline strategy with RB Tyrone Tracy Jr. on IR
item.description: The New York Giants placed running back Tyrone Tracy Jr. on injured reserve Tuesday with a hamstring injury.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The New York Giants placed running back Tyrone Tracy Jr. on injured reserve Tuesday with a hamstring injury. Tracy sustained the injury during the second quarter of New York's 27-21 overtime victory over the Houston Texans on Sunday. The move will sideline Tracy for at least four games for the Giants (4-2-1), who will return from their bye week to visit the reeling Philadelphia Eagles on Nov. 8. Schoen said the injury is not considered season-ending, but the Giants did sign former Memphis running back Greg Desrosiers off the Los Angeles Chargers' practice squad. Tracy, 26, has rushed 19 times for 55 yards and two touchdowns this season. He has rushed for 1,634 yards and nine touchdowns in 39 career games (23 starts) with New York since being drafted in the fifth round in 2024. With Tracy sidelined, Devin Singletary likely will receive a few more carries as he backs up Cam Skattebo in the backfield. The Giants also have Phil Mafah on their practice squad, so Schoen said Tracy's injury does not change the team's approach to the trade deadline. Without fourth- or fifth-round picks in next year's draft, Schoen said that could factor into players the team might be interested in at various positions ahead of the trade deadline. "It's easy to say, 'go sign X, Y, and Z position,' but if a team's really not ready to get rid of somebody where they're asking too much, it doesn't match up with where you see the value, then it doesn't make sense to do it," Schoen said. "We're going to look at all the options that are available. And there's certain teams that have already started some trades and we've been in contact with those teams and have a pretty good idea of who may or may not be available. And again, it's got to make sense, short-term and long-term, when you make those moves." The Giants parted with next year's fourth-round selection as part of a package of picks sent to Cleveland to move up to draft wide receiver Malachi Fields. The fifth-rounder was sent to Minnesota to acquire quarterback J.J. McCarthy. "The utilization of those draft picks that we gave up to get those two players, we're happy we have them," Schoen said. "There are always options to regain capital down the road. "If it makes sense right now for us to do something in the short-term and long-term, we're going to look at any opportunity that we can to upgrade the roster. And, again, there's avenues that we can try to recoup draft picks down the road." --Field Level Media

item.title: Hackers target US FEC system, disrupting campaign finance disclosures days before midterms
item.description: The US Federal Election Commission's website has been targeted by a hacker or hackers, according to an email seen by Reuters, disrupting the agency's electronic filings system a week before the November 3 elections.
item.dc:creator: Dawn Kopecki
item.content:encoded: The US Federal Election Commission's website has been targeted by a hacker or hackers, according to an email seen by Reuters, disrupting the agency's electronic filings system a week before the November 3 elections. The cyberattack comes as so-called super PACs and dark money groups spend record sums in the final days of the races. The elections will determine whether President Donald Trump's Republicans maintain their majorities in Congress for the next two years. In a statement, the FEC said, "at this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service." The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said users could still search the website for past reports. It declined further comment on the outage. The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots. The outage prevents organizations from filing the FEC's 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which show how much political groups and others are spending on specific races. "I've never seen this in 26 years," said Steven Mele, president and CEO at political finance compliance firm MBA Consulting Group. "The result is there will be less disclosure on the elections" until it's fixed. A status message posted by the FEC said its filing system had been down since around 10 p.m. ET on Monday (0200 GMT Tuesday). The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions to the FEC. The FBI did not immediately return messages seeking comment. The FEC posted the notice after campaign finance officers couldn't file mandatory reports late on Monday. "We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily shut down our web facing services," an FEC electronic filings officer said in the email to several campaign compliance firms that night. The midterms are now the most expensive US election in history with roughly $11.21 billion spent on advertising and future reservations so far, according to political ad tracker AdImpact. It's surpassed the previous record set in the 2024 elections when $11.2 billion was spent on all races, including $3.2 billion on the presidential race between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris, AdImpact said. Much of the spending is being driven by super PACs, which can accept unlimited amounts of money from wealthy individuals and corporations and spend as much as they want on campaigns with few restrictions. The sums being spent in recent weeks are staggering as Democrats gain ground in several Republican strongholds. Super PACs and dark money groups have spent an average of over $50 million per day over the last week, said Brendan Glavin, research director at nonpartisan campaign watchdog group OpenSecrets. More than $250 million in spending was reported on October 20 alone, he added. "It's a big deal," he said of the outage, which leaves voters in the dark until the filing system is back online. "These are the key reports that tell us what is happening," Glavin said. "In the last days of the election this is the only way for us to keep track of where the money's being spent" and who's spending it.

item.title: US agency approves Amazon Leo’s $11.5 billion acquisition of Globalstar
item.description: The Federal Communications Commission said on Tuesday it approved Amazon Leo’s $11.5 billion deal to acquire Globalstar as the retail giant's satellite arm seeks to build a communications network to compete with SpaceX's Starlink .
item.dc:creator: David Shepardson
item.content:encoded: The Federal Communications Commission said on Tuesday it approved Amazon (AMZN.O) Leo’s $11.5 billion deal to acquire Globalstar (GSAT.O) as the retail giant's satellite arm seeks to build a communications network to compete with SpaceX's Starlink (SPCX.O) . Amazon Leo has launched nearly 400 satellites since April 2025 and aims to deploy thousands of satellites in Earth's low orbit by 2029. Through the deal, Amazon adds Globalstar's two dozen satellites and its mobile-satellite spectrum. Amazon, which has committed to investing more than $10 billion in Leo, is preparing to roll out its commercial satellite services by the end of 2026, the FCC said. The FCC said the companies’ assets will boost Amazon Leo’s entry into the direct-to-device market and allow the satellite operator to offer fixed and mobile services. "The FCC has empowered Amazon Leo to deliver fast, next-gen satellite broadband services, increase competition, and help communities stay connected all across the country," FCC Chair Brendan Carr said. Tech companies are pouring billions of dollars into capturing the lucrative market for satellite-based connectivity as they race to compete with Starlink's network of more than 11,000 satellites. Amazon praised the approval, saying it "brings us a step closer to bringing new connectivity capabilities to customers." Amazon in July sought [USN:L4N43T10V TEXT:"approval from the FCC for up to 5,105"] satellites. Direct-to-device satellite technology allows smartphones and other devices to connect directly to satellites. The FCC will vote on Thursday to advance a new auction of wireless spectrum to boost "direct-to-device" services. Globalstar currently powers satellite-based safety features such as Emergency SOS and Find My for Apple's (AAPL.O) iPhone and Apple Watch users. Amazon said earlier that it has signed an agreement with Apple to continue providing those services. Apple invested about $1.5 billion in Globalstar in 2024 to fund the expansion of its iPhone communication services, in a deal that also gave the tech giant a 20% equity stake in Globalstar. Apple accounted for about 63% of Globalstar's revenue last year and Amazon plans to acquire Apple's stake, the FCC said. Globalstar said late last year that a new, Apple-backed network under development would expand its footprint to 54 satellites, including a small number of backups, from the two dozen currently.

item.title: Mexico's electoral body pledges internal overhaul after corruption crisis
item.description: Mexico's National Electoral Institute (INE) promised on Tuesday to carry out an exhaustive, independent and transparent overhaul to guarantee its continuity, after its chief resigned over allegations of irregularities and corruption.
item.dc:creator: Raul Cortes
item.content:encoded: Mexico's National Electoral Institute (INE) promised on Tuesday to carry out an exhaustive, independent and transparent overhaul to guarantee its continuity, after its chief resigned over allegations of irregularities and corruption. The leadership [USN:L2N46C0L2 TEXT:"upheaval"] raises fresh questions over the credibility and stability of the autonomous authority as it prepares to oversee Mexico's 2027 midterm elections. Lawmakers face the task of choosing a permanent successor to Guadalupe Taddei to steer the INE through an increasingly contentious political environment. "It is a good time for whoever takes office to exercise transparency and ensure that no department within the National Electoral Institute favors any particular side, and that the Institute fulfills its duties," Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said at her daily press conference. INE's top members announced several measures to overcome the crisis at an unusual press conference led by Blanca Cruz, who earlier was named as interim president. Her designation is due to be formalized later on Tuesday. Cruz, an electoral adviser, joined the INE's General Council in April. "The provisional presidency has a clear responsibility: to facilitate dialogue, ensure institutional continuity, and contribute to the decisions that are being shaped through deliberation and consensus," Cruz said at the press conference. Taddei [USN:L2N46C0L2 TEXT:"resigned"] on Monday in the most high-profile departure tied to alleged corruption in Sheinbaum's two-year-old presidency. Sheinbaum said she supported Taddei's decision. Mexico's Superior Audit Office is investigating alleged irregularities involving INE contracts, including possible conflicts of interest and the triangulation of public funds. Taddei, in local news outlets, has been accused of favoring an INE contractor, with whom she has a personal relationship, with contracts worth millions of dollars. Cruz said the INE council was reviewing officials in decision-making roles, adding that three senior officials had already resigned: the heads of IT Services and the Gender Equality and Non-Discrimination Unit, and the official responsible for material resources. Local media described all three as members of Taddei’s inner circle. Taddei has not spoken publicly since resigning. "Over the past few days, rumors, fabricated material, leaks, and versions of events have spread through the media and social networks, and as in all such cases, their authenticity, context, and purpose must be verified and corroborated," she said in a statement on Sunday announcing her planned resignation.

item.title: Constellation gets conditional loan up to $5 billion for US nuclear plant upgrades
item.description: Constellation Energy said on Tuesday it received a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion from the US Department of Energy to fund upgrades of nuclear plants in three states that will help it generate more power.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Gardner, Pranav Mathur
item.content:encoded: Constellation Energy (CEG.O) said on Tuesday it received a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion from the US Department of Energy to fund upgrades of nuclear plants in three states that will help it generate more power. US demand for power is growing for the first time in decades due to AI data center expansion, electrification of transportation and cryptocurrency mining. President Donald Trump set a goal to quadruple US nuclear power capacity by 2050. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said his department's loan office has [USN:L1N3WM0OV TEXT:"hundreds of billions"] of dollars in financing available, most of which is expected to support nuclear plants. The upgrades, known in the industry as uprates, increase power generation from existing reactors through changes such as more efficient components, without needing new licenses from the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Licensing has in the past taken years. The potential financing will help Constellation fund uprates at eight facilities in Illinois, Maryland and Pennsylvania, to add nearly 1.1 gigawatts of capacity. That is enough electricity to power more than 930,000 homes, the department said. CONSTELLATION SHARES CLIMB Shares in Maryland-based Constellation, the largest US nuclear power plant operator, rose 2.6%. The company said the financing could reduce borrowing costs and speed up projects without building new plants or laying down transmission lines. Wright, who made the announcement at Constellation's Byron plant in Illinois, said that site's capacity could increase by 150 megawatts, up from nearly 2.35 GW from two reactors. "All the infrastructure is here — we're just changing out some turbines and getting more energy out of it," Wright told Fox News. Earlier this month, the Energy Department announced a conditional loan commitment of about [USN:L1N45P034 TEXT:"$4.2 billion"] for upgrades at Vistra Corp (VST.N) nuclear power plants. According to the NRC, utilities can uprate nuclear plants by refueling with slightly more enriched uranium or through major plant modifications such as replacing main turbines. Utilities have used uprates to generate more power from reactors since the 1970s. The conditional loan commitment includes an option to finance future uprates at additional Constellation facilities, the Energy Department's loan office said.

item.title: Judge hears Justice Dept suit claiming noncitizens on California voter rolls
item.description: A US judge heard arguments on Tuesday on the Justice Department's request to block California from counting any mail ballots for the November 3 midterm elections from more than 20,000 registered voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens.
item.dc:creator: Luc Cohen, Jan Wolfe
item.content:encoded: A US judge heard arguments on Tuesday on the Justice Department's request to block California from counting any mail ballots for the November 3 midterm elections from more than 20,000 registered voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens. The Justice Department's October 15 lawsuit marked an escalation in President Donald Trump 's effort to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the midterms, with his Republican Party locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress. The lawsuit is a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election. The US Constitution assigns the responsibility of administering elections to individual states, though the federal government has some oversight role. US District Judge David Carter held a court hearing in Los Angeles to consider the department's request for a temporary restraining order barring officials from [USN:L6N46117W TEXT:"counting any ballots"] from the individuals it flagged. Cartrer ended the three-hour hearing without making a ruling, but told lawyers he would issue it on Wednesday. California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust. Anne Bellows, a lawyer for California, said during Tuesday's hearing that the Justice Department's assertions relied on "mysterious database methods" and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters. "The Supreme Court has reiterated time and again that, as an election is close at hand, federal courts should not interfere to change the rules under which that election is held," Bellows added. "This applies with even more force when the election is ongoing." Justice Department lawyer Bilal Essayli countered that the federal government had made a narrow request to ensure election integrity. California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state. Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its "sanctuary state" policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. Trump has repeatedly insisted that states are not doing enough to stop voting by noncitizens, which he says is widespread despite multiple studies and state audits showing it is rare. ADDITIONAL TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ACTIONS The hearing comes after a federal appeals court on Monday [USN:L2N46C163 TEXT:"rejected"] an unusual emergency request by the Justice Department asking the appeals court to temporarily block California from counting the ballots before Carter had the chance to rule. The Justice Department did not indicate how many of the more than 20,000 people it flagged in California had actually submitted a mail ballot. Apart from California, the Trump administration has sought to intervene in elections in two states that are home to [USN:L6N4670ZS TEXT:"competitive races"]. In Alaska, the Justice Department last week asked a judge to [USN:L2N46D019 TEXT:"prevent certification"] of election results if the Republican incumbent senator loses by a slim margin, alleging that the presence of another candidate with a similar name on the ballot could confuse voters. Alaska has urged that the case be dismissed, arguing it has taken steps to distinguish the two candidates on the ballot. In Washington state, the Justice Department on Monday [USN:L6N46D0UP TEXT:"sent a letter"] asking officials not to count any ballots received from 400 voters it said may not be citizens. Washington's top elections official said the timing of the request indicated it was intended to cast unfounded suspicion on election results. California had 23 million registered voters as of December 2025, while Washington had 5 million registered voters as of 2024, state records show. Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the federal government's methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizen voters risk wrongly flagging naturalized citizens for removal from the rolls.

item.title: Trump says he will visit tanker in Texas with first oil from Venezuela deal
item.description: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he planned to visit a tanker in Texas which contains the first oil received from Venezuela following a deal that Washington made after deposing the country's former leader.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he planned to visit a tanker in Texas which contains the first oil received from Venezuela following a deal that Washington made after deposing the country's former leader. [USN:FWN44P1ZC TEXT:"Trump announced in August an agreement"] that grants the United States access to a fifth of Venezuela's crude reserves. "They've sent me as a gift a boatload of a million barrels of oil, and I'm giving that to the United States of America," Trump told reporters. He later said in a post on Truth Social that this was the "first shipment of BILLIONS of Barrels to come." The White House said in September that oil from the Venezuela deal would probably hit US reserves in November. The United States has been working closely with the interim government led by acting President Delcy Rodriguez since US forces captured President Nicolas Maduro in January.

item.title: Flávio Bolsonaro viaja para os EUA após derrota na eleição; Departamento de Estado dará vistos para família
item.description: Flávio Bolsonaro viajou para os Estados Unidos nesta terça-feira, disseram à Reuters um aliado próximo do parlamentar e uma fonte do governo dos EUA, menos de 24 horas após o senador assegurar que nunca pensara em deixar o país e depois da derrota eleitoral no domingo para o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Brito, Gram Slattery
item.content:encoded: Flávio Bolsonaro viajou para os Estados Unidos nesta terça-feira, disseram à Reuters um aliado próximo do parlamentar e uma fonte do governo dos EUA, menos de 24 horas após o senador assegurar que nunca pensara em deixar o país e depois da derrota eleitoral no domingo para o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. O Departamento de Estado dos Estados Unidos emitirá vistos para Flávio e sua família e permitirá a entrada deles nos EUA, disse uma autoridade sênior do órgão à Reuters. Segundo um aliado da família Bolsonaro disse à Reuters que o senador chegou ao Estado da Flórida, nos EUA. O ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) havia determinado que Flávio entregasse seus passaportes até o final da manhã, o que não foi feito, e que ele estava proibido de deixar o país. A decisão se deu no âmbito de um inquérito em que o senador é investigado por lavagem de dinheiro juntamente com o advogado Willer Tomaz, seu amigo. Ambos os investigados negam qualquer irregularidade. No início da noite, Lula criticou a decisão de seu adversário na disputa eleitoral de sair do país "Ato vergonhoso. Se fugiu é porque teme, porque quem não deve não teme", disse o presidente, em ato com aliados e apoiadores de comemoração pelos seus 81 anos. O governo do presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, já alegou que o pai de Flávio, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, foi vítima de perseguição judicial no Brasil. Jair Bolsonaro foi condenado a 27 anos de prisão por tentativa de golpe de Estado. SURPRESA Na véspera, o candidato derrotado na eleição de domingo afirmara que nunca pensara em deixar o país. "Eu nunca pensei em sair do país. Eu vou entregar os meus passaportes e vou me defender dessa aberração, que é uma clara tentativa de me intimidar", disse Flávio em vídeo publicado em sua conta no Instagram na segunda-feira, afirmando ainda que organizaria a oposição ao governo Lula. Antes da votação de domingo, o ex-deputado Eduardo Bolsonaro, irmão de Flávio, afirmou em uma transmissão nas redes sociais que Flávio deveria deixar o país caso perdesse a eleição presidencial. Moraes citou risco de fuga e "expressivo poder econômico" dos envolvidos na decisão que determinou a apreensão do passaporte do senador, segundo a decisão vista pela Reuters. Em entrevista no início da noite desta terça, após participar de uma reunião da cúpula do PL, o coordenador-geral da campanha de Flávio, o senador Rogério Marinho (RN), disse que não tinha informação sobre o paradeiro dele. "Estamos surpresos porque ontem (segunda) conversamos sobre a necessidade de Flávio, com quase 60 milhões de votos que teve, assumisse esse papel de liderança da oposição", afirmou ele, acrescentando que tinha recebido uma mensagem de texto mais cedo que dizia que Flávio iria "dar um tempo". PASSOS DO PAI A viagem de Flávio para os Estados Unidos repetiria os passos do pai, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, que viajou para os Estados Unidos depois de se recusar a reconhecer a derrota para Lula na eleição presidencial de 2022. Jair Bolsonaro acabou retornando ao Brasil, mas posteriormente foi condenado a 27 anos de prisão por tentativa de golpe de Estado. Flávio ainda não reconheceu oficialmente a derrota no domingo. No dia da votação, afirmou que buscaria a anulação do resultado alegando irregularidades após a prorrogação do prazo de votação. Posteriormente, disse que pediria a cassação da chapa de Lula ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). No entanto, seu partido, o PL, declarou na segunda-feira que reconhecia a vitória de Lula.

item.title: El Salvador rushes some 1,000 troops to Haiti after gang ambush, source says
item.description: El Salvador has sent about 1,000 troops to Haiti after four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed security mission went missing in a gang ambush on the outskirts of the capital on October 18, a security official in Haiti told Reuters on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Morland
item.content:encoded: El Salvador has sent about 1,000 troops to Haiti after four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed security mission went missing in a gang ambush on the outskirts of the capital on October 18, a security official in Haiti told Reuters on Tuesday. The troops' arrival aboard flights in recent days dramatically expands the Central American nation's role in Haiti's long-standing gang conflict. Yet it remains unclear who will command the new Salvadoran contingent, how long it will stay in Haiti or whether more forces will follow. Neither the Haitian nor Salvadoran government immediately responded to requests for comment. The official in Haiti spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the security situation. The deployment comes as the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force has reached about 2,000 personnel, just over a third of its planned strength a year into its mandate, with little improvement in Haiti's security. Armed gangs in Haiti have meanwhile expanded their influence over the capital and surrounding regions through extortion and [USN:S0N43903K TEXT:"brutal attacks"] that have displaced nearly 1.5 million people. Haiti's leaders have sought international security support since 2022, despite the country's fraught history of foreign intervention. Gangs' influence grew rapidly after the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise, deepening an insecurity crisis that has caused authorities to repeatedly delay elections. Pierre Esperance, head of Haiti's National Human Rights Defense Network, welcomed the unusually rapid Salvadoran deployment and said he hoped it would help stop gangs from terrorizing civilians. But he warned that any operation must avoid harming residents trapped in gang-held neighborhoods. "Not everybody living in gang-controlled areas are gangsters," he said. President Nayib Bukele last week announced a military operation to recover the missing Salvadorans, who remain unaccounted for since jumping from a burning vehicle during the ambush. He has not said how many troops would be sent. The US provided C-130 transport aircraft to help move Salvadoran troops to Haiti, a US military official said. Additional commercial and military flights between San Salvador and Port-au-Prince were visible on flight-tracking site Flightradar24 and were also reported by the Miami Herald. A photo posted on X on Tuesday by a lawmaker from Bukele's ruling party showed a plane carrying uniformed soldiers, some taking selfies. NO CLAIM OF RESPONSIBILITY Bukele has built strong domestic support through a hardline anti-crime campaign that several right-wing governments in the Americas have sought to emulate. Human rights groups however warn that the crackdown has come at the cost of [USN:L6N41418X TEXT:"due process"] and has been linked to hundreds of deaths in custody. Bukele said the missing Salvadorans were air force technicians, returning to base from a market, and that he believed they were being [USN:L1N46712A TEXT:"held hostage"] by criminal groups. No Haitian gang has claimed responsibility for the ambush. Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, has released videos denying that his group is holding the Salvadorans or was involved in the attack. Before the ambush, El Salvador had deployed at least 124 personnel to the force. Bukele said they were pilots and technicians sent to evacuate wounded personnel, not combatants. Alongside the international mission, Haiti's government has also hired a private military company run by [USN:L1N43N12B TEXT:"Blackwater founder"] Erik Prince - an ally of US President Donald Trump - which has since 2025 carried out controversial anti-gang drone operations. Luis Contreras, a Salvadoran security and organized crime analyst, said he expected that at least some of the new troops would operate outside the UN-backed mission's chain of command and could coordinate with Prince's firm. "The UN has lacked the political will to resolve the issue of the gangs in Haiti," he said. "Once the whereabouts of the four members have been established, they will have to assess whether to engage in a direct and protracted confrontation."

item.title: JetBlue CEO says no creditor talks as bond selloff raises doubts about turnaround
item.description: JetBlue Airways is not in talks with creditors and is not planning to restructure its debt, Chief Executive Joanna Geraghty told Reuters on Tuesday, after a sharp selloff in the airline's bonds raised concerns about its finances.
item.dc:creator: Doyinsola Oladipo
item.content:encoded: JetBlue Airways (JBLU.O) is not in talks with creditors and is not planning to restructure its debt, Chief Executive Joanna Geraghty told Reuters on Tuesday, after a sharp selloff in the airline's bonds raised concerns about its finances. Geraghty's comments come days after a group of creditors hired restructuring advisers PJT Partners and Akin Gump, according to media reports, raising questions about the carrier's ability to fund a turnaround without having to renegotiate its debt. The airline, which has about $8.4 billion in debt and finance lease obligations, has not posted an annual profit since 2019 and reported on Monday that its third-quarter net loss deepened to $257 million from $143 million a year earlier primarily due to soaring fuel costs. "We are not in talks with our creditors," Geraghty said. "Part of today, as I mentioned, was to really set the record straight that we're making progress in the underlying business." When asked if the airline was pursuing any financial support from the US government, Geraghty said it was not. She also reiterated that debt restructuring was not under consideration. Separately, Geraghty met with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week to discuss a range of issues, according to a person briefed on the matter. JetBlue declined to comment on whether the meeting occurred. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company's roughly $2 billion in bonds backed by its TrueBlue frequent-flyer program were trading at about $47 for every $100 of debt on October 26, down from around $80 at the start of the month, according to LSEG data. The steep drop pushed yields, the returns investors demand for holding the bonds, above 30%, signaling concerns about the airline's ability to repay its debt because of volatile fuel costs. Fuel expenses jumped 61% in the third quarter but the company said it was able to recover 87% of that as fares rose across the industry with no meaningful decline in passenger volume. The airline said in its quarterly filing that a 10% rise in fuel prices would increase its fuel costs by about $376 million over the next year, based on its projected fuel consumption. Revenue in the period rose by more than a fifth to $2.8 billion. "Our results tell a very different story from what our bondholders are communicating out there in the market," she said in an interview. JetBlue stock closed up 19% on Tuesday, but it is down 38% so far this year. FUNDING THE TURNAROUND JetBlue used $273 million in cash from operations in the first nine months of 2026, nearly double the $143 million a year earlier. Its unrestricted cash and investments fell about $850 million from December to $1.6 billion at September-end, partly reflecting aircraft purchases, and its working-capital deficit widened to $1.6 billion from $1.2 billion at the end of last year. The airline faces scheduled debt and finance lease repayments of $477 million in 2027 and $582 million in 2028, before a larger $1.8 billion comes due in 2029, according to its quarterly filing. It paid $372 million in net cash interest in the first nine months of the year. JetBlue reported $2.2 billion in liquidity and about $7 billion in assets not already pledged to lenders that could help it raise additional funds, and said in the filing it had enough liquidity to meet its needs for at least the next 12 months. About two-thirds of its owned property, equipment and intangible assets by book value were already pledged under various loan agreements. The company expects another $250 million in aircraft-backed financing in the fourth quarter. On Tuesday's earnings call, Geraghty identified potential funding sources beyond traditional borrowing, including JetBlue's Paisly travel business, venture investments and co-branded credit-card partnership, but gave no details of any specific plans. JetBlue now expects a full-year adjusted operating margin of negative 4.5% to negative 6.5%, worse than the negative 2% to negative 5% forecast in July. The airline still aims to return to operating profitability in 2027 and generate positive free cash flow in 2028.

item.title: Rights monitors raise concerns over senior UAE diplomat bid for next UN boss
item.description: Human rights monitors criticized senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh's candidacy to be the next UN chief on Tuesday, citing her role in championing the country's foreign policy and denying the UAE's role in fuelling the conflict in Sudan.
item.dc:creator: Antoni Slodkowski
item.content:encoded: Human rights monitors criticized senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh's candidacy to be the next UN chief on Tuesday, citing her role in championing the country's foreign policy and denying the UAE's role in fuelling the conflict in Sudan. Pushback against the prominent Middle Eastern candidate has gathered steam since her late entry last week. Her bid upended the gridlocked race to replace UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year. Despite [USN:L1N4620XQ TEXT:"months of campaigning"] by several senior UN figures and former country leaders, the competition has struggled to produce a consensus choice among the Security Council’s most powerful nations. Sudan's war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. "She has been asked about the UAE's role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts — that is not what we need as UN Secretary-General," Kenneth Roth, former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told a webinar organized by online campaigns group Avaaz. Last month, a [USN:L6N44U158 TEXT:"UN fact-finding mission said"] foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks -- including individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, among others -- are helping sustain Sudan's conflict. "This is the opposite of the kind of moral standing of the human rights leadership that we want from a UN Secretary-General," Roth told the webinar titled "Call To Stop UAE Minister's Bid for UN Top Job Amid Sudan Genocide". The webinar also featured Sudanese experts, as well as a survivor of the El Fasher massacre , on their concerns about Nusseibeh's candidacy and its implications for the UN's commitment to protect civilians, according to the organizers. "Electing (the UAE's) senior diplomat as Secretary-General would hand leadership of (United Nations) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable," said Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV. Asked about Sudan during the dialogue with the General Assembly on Tuesday, Nusseibeh said: "If I were to become secretary-general, Sudan would be a number one priority, as one of the most horrific conflicts we have seen in recent history." "The loss of human life on the ground is a tragedy, the atrocities committed by the RSF are atrocious, and I would support the work of all UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice," she added. Nusseibeh told the media at the UN after the dialogue that, as a secretary-general, she would work to be a "risk-taker" and "prime mover in mediation efforts." She has also separately said she would "put the UN's full political and practical support behind ongoing efforts to reach a ceasefire and a credible and inclusive political process that reflects the democratic aspirations of the Sudanese people." Nusseibeh served as UAE ambassador to the UN for more than a decade. She previously led the UAE's successful campaign for election to the Security Council as a non-permanent member in 2022-23. She is widely known by diplomats working in New York, who say she is a competent manager, skilled negotiator and clear communicator. An informal council poll this month [USN:L1N4620XQ TEXT:"had placed"] former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the ultimately decisive five permanent members of the council — Russia, China, the US, France and Britain. Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN, and the 193-member body's declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

item.title: Trump promotes oil production in Texas, where Democrats dream of breakthrough
item.description: President Donald Trump campaigned in the traditionally solidly Republican state of Texas on Tuesday, seeking to boost US Senate candidate Ken Paxton and other party members and fend off what could be the first statewide Democratic victory in 32 years.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump campaigned in the traditionally solidly Republican state of Texas on Tuesday, seeking to boost US Senate candidate Ken Paxton and other party members and fend off what could be the first statewide Democratic victory in 32 years. With high fuel prices weighing heavily on the campaign for November 3 congressional elections, Trump scheduled a pair of stops at opposite ends of the oil-producing state. He appeared before a tanker containing Venezuelan crude in the Gulf of Mexico, and planned to announce the easing of methane rules for oil and gas producers during a later stop in the West Texas city of Lubbock. Trump sought to show voters he was working to bring down gasoline prices a week before the midterm elections, when the balance of power in Congress will be at stake. Polls show the Democrats may retake control of one or both houses from the president's Republicans. Trump has taken a number of steps to [USN:L1N4670FM TEXT:"address fuel prices"], which have become a political liability for Republicans amid the US war with Iran. The trip marks Trump's third visit to Texas this month to mobilize support for Paxton, who is locked in a close race with Democrat James Talarico. A loss in Texas next Tuesday would complicate the Republican Party's path to retaining its slim Senate majority. The rally took place within view of an oil tanker, moored near the Port of Corpus Christi, that Trump said was loaded with the first oil received from Venezuela under a deal that Washington made after deposing the country's former leader. "We're celebrating the greatest oil victory in history. To the victor belongs the spoils, right?" Trump said. Texas has long been one of the main refining centers for Venezuelan crude oil. [USN:FWN44P1ZC TEXT:"Trump announced in August an agreement"] that grants the US access to a fifth of Venezuela's crude reserves. The White House said in September that oil from the deal would probably hit US reserves in November. The oil is slated to head to refineries owned by ExxonMobil and Citgo, a White House official told Reuters. LATE PUSH FOR PAXTON Texas has consistently voted Republican for 30 years, but Democrats raised their hopes this year when Paxton won the Senate nomination with Trump's backing. Paxton was indicted on securities-fraud charges in 2015 and impeached by the Texas House in 2023. The criminal case was dismissed in 2024 after an agreement with prosecutors, and the Texas Senate acquitted him in the impeachment trial. Trump has publicly criticized his longtime ally Paxton, calling him "a pain in the ass sometimes." He also heavily criticized Talarico, whom he accused of opposing Texas values on issues such as oil production, immigration and transgender rights. Tech billionaire Elon Musk and other donors are [USN:L6N4660XW TEXT:"pouring hundreds of millions"] into a late effort to rescue Paxton's campaign. "Our policy has always been drill, baby, drill. And man, we are drilling now. But if Texas elects Communist James 'Talafreako,' that wealth will rapidly disappear," Trump said, applying his preferred nickname to the Democratic candidate. Talarico has used the nickname as a fundraising tool, selling 'I'm a Talafreako' T-shirts, while also responding, "We are a threat to their corrupt system." During a later stop in Lubbock, Trump was expected to announce an Environmental Protection Agency proposal to roll back Biden-era rules that required companies to fix leaky equipment and regularly check wells for escaping methane, a potent greenhouse gas, the White House official said. The administration is casting it as a way to produce more energy and lower costs. The plan would give relief to small, low-output wells and end a program that used outside groups to report large methane leaks, the official said. It would also ease rules aimed at phasing out the routine burning off of gas at oil wells. Trump's repeated trips to Texas are part of a broader push in Republican-leaning states, which were expected to be safely in hand but have instead become midterm battlegrounds. His October campaign blitz has also taken him to Oklahoma, Alabama, Nebraska, Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Mississippi.

item.title: US Supreme Court denies immigration judges the power to shelve deportation cases
item.description: The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump's administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Chung
item.content:encoded: The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump 's administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice. The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities including Baltimore and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as "administrative closure," while litigation continues in the dispute. The Supreme Court's decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from the decision. The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day. Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule's invalidation. In a statement, the litigants and the lawyers representing them from the liberal legal group Democracy Forward expressed disappointment in Tuesday's decision. "Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country," they said in the statement. "This dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny," they added. Representatives from the Justice Department and the Texas attorney general's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction. Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty. HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF CASES Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump's hardline approach toward immigrants. In 2024, Biden's administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a prior rule adopted in 2020 during Trump's first term in office that had been judicially blocked. After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department office that oversees immigration courts, the Executive Office for Immigration Review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge. In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges "effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country." Trump's administration and the state then jointly asked US District Judge Reed O'Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O'Connor did so, blocking it permanently, nationwide. Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider, Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend the rule, but O'Connor rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations. The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O'Connor's decision. The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told the Supreme Court in a filing that Trump's administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using "manufactured litigation" with "ideologically aligned" Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked. "The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception," they wrote.

item.title: Flavio Bolsonaro and family to receive US visas after leaving Brazil, State Department says
item.description: Lula, speaking in Brasilia, said he had just heard that Flavio had left the country, and called it shameful, saying he should have stayed in Brazil and proved his innocence.
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Brito, Gram Slattery, Luciana Novaes Magalhaes
item.content:encoded: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after losing Sunday's presidential election, three sources said on Tuesday afternoon, with the US State Department due to grant him and his family entry visas. Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left Brazil after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports. The ruling relates to a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing. The location of Flavio, his wife and two daughters was not immediately clear. One source close to the family said Flavio had landed in Florida, but declined to say where. "The State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States," a senior State Department official said. BRAZIL-US RIFT GROWS Bolsonaro's departure threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. Lula has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaros to put them back in power, and Reuters reported ahead of Sunday's election on [USN:L1N4650X8 TEXT:"a US State Department"] campaign to restore them to office. Trump has previously alleged Flavio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil. The elder Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former US President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia. Trump made no mention of Flavio Bolsonaro's departure in comments to the press on Monday, but said the Brazilian vote "looked like another rigged election." Lula, speaking in Brasilia, said he had just heard that Flavio had left the country, and called it shameful, saying he should have stayed in Brazil and proved his innocence. Bolsonaro was favored to win Sunday's presidential election but ended up [USN:L2N46B01X TEXT:"losing"] in a shock result to Lula. ORDERED TO HAND OVER PASSPORTS On Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports, but they were canceled after the deadline lapsed, two sources said. In a court ruling seen by Reuters, the Supreme Court cited the risk of Bolsonaro fleeing Brazil and his "significant financial resources" in ordering his passports seized. Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, said on Monday he had no plans to flee. "I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me." His departure appeared to have caught his campaign manager off guard. "We are surprised by the news because, just yesterday, we discussed the need for Flavio — given the 60 million votes he received — to take on this role as leader of the opposition," Senator Rogerio Marinho told reporters. FOLLOWING FATHER'S PATH Although Bolsonaro has yet to officially concede defeat — saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities — his Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula's victory. It remains unclear how Bolsonaro was able to leave the country while he was facing a 24-hour deadline to hand over his passports. A senior Federal Police official said Bolsonaro had not exited the country via any regular migration point. Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro's younger brother who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote that an election loss would require a move. "If my brother does not win, I'm in favor that he would leave the country," he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month.

item.title: Flávio Bolsonaro y familia recibirán visas EEUU tras abandonar Brasil: Departamento Estado
item.description: El senador Flávio Bolsonaro abandonó Brasil con destino a Estados Unidos tras perder las elecciones presidenciales del domingo, informaron tres fuentes, mientras que el Departamento de Estado le concederá visados de entrada a él y su familia.
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Brito, Gram Slattery
item.content:encoded: El senador Flávio Bolsonaro abandonó Brasil con destino a Estados Unidos tras perder las elecciones presidenciales del domingo, informaron tres fuentes, mientras que el Departamento de Estado le concederá visados de entrada a él y su familia. Bolsonaro, que aún no ha reconocido su derrota ante Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, abandonó Brasil tras negarse a acatar una orden del Supremo Tribunal Federal de entregar sus pasaportes, una decisión relacionada con una investigación por blanqueo de dinero en la que él niega haber cometido delito alguno. Se desconocía de inmediato el paradero de Flavio, su esposa y sus dos hijas. Una fuente cercana a la familia indicó que había aterrizado en Florida, pero se negó a precisar el lugar. "El Departamento de Estado expedirá visados a Flavio Bolsonaro y su familia y les permitirá la entrada a Estados Unidos", declaró un funcionario de alto rango del Departamento de Estado. La partida de Flávio Bolsonaro amenaza con profundizar la brecha entre las dos naciones más pobladas de América. Lula ha acusado a Washington de confabularse con los Bolsonaro para devolverlos al poder. Reuters informó antes de las elecciones del domingo sobre una campaña del Departamento de Estado de Estados Unidos para restituirlos en sus cargos. UN "ACTO VERGONZOSO" Lula calificó como un "acto vergonzoso" el hecho de que su adversario haya salido del país rumbo a Estados Unidos. El mandatario afirmó, en un discurso ante sus simpatizantes con motivo de su cumpleaños número 81, que "quien nada debe, nada teme", y argumentó que el senador debe tener cargo de conciencia para haber decidido abandonar el país tras la derrota. El presidente Donald Trump ya había alegado que el padre de Flavio, el expresidente Jair Bolsonaro, fue víctima de persecución judicial en Brasil. Jair Bolsonaro también se trasladó a Estados Unidos tras haberse negado a reconocer su derrota frente a Lula en 2022, durante el mandato de Joe Biden. Luego regresó a Brasil, pero fue condenado a 27 años de prisión por conspirar para dar un golpe de Estado, luego de que sus seguidores irrumpieron en edificios gubernamentales en Brasilia. Trump no hizo mención alguna a la salida de Flávio Bolsonaro en sus declaraciones a la prensa el lunes, pero dijo que los comicios brasileños "parecían otra elección amañada". La oficina de Lula no respondió a una solicitud de comentarios. Bolsonaro era el favorito para ganar el domingo, pero acabó perdiendo por sorpresa frente a Lula. El lunes se le concedieron 24 horas para entregar su pasaporte como parte de una investigación por blanqueo de capitales, en la que él niega haber cometido algún delito, pero el plazo ya venció, indicaron otras dos fuentes, lo que ha llevado a la anulación de sus documentos. Bolsonaro, que perderá su inmunidad judicial cuando finalice su mandato en el Senado en febrero, había dicho el lunes que no tenía intención de huir. "Nunca he pensado en salir del país", dijo. "Entregaré mis pasaportes y me defenderé contra esta farsa, que es un claro intento de intimidarme". Su marcha pareció pillar desprevenido a su jefe de campaña. "Nos sorprende la noticia porque, precisamente ayer, hablamos de la necesidad de que Flavio, dados los 60 millones de votos que recibió, asumiera el papel de líder de la oposición", declaró a la prensa el senador Rogerio Marinho. Flávio Bolsonaro aún no ha reconocido oficialmente la derrota -el domingo anunció que solicitaría la anulación del resultado por supuestas irregularidades electorales-, pero su Partido Liberal declaró el lunes que reconocía la victoria de Lula. Sigue sin estar claro cómo logró Bolsonaro salir del país mientras pesaba sobre él una orden del STF (la corte suprema local) que le daba un plazo de 24 horas para entregar sus pasaportes. Un alto cargo de la Policía Federal brasileña dijo que Bolsonaro no abandonó el país a través de ningún punto migratorio oficial. Eduardo Bolsonaro, el hermano menor de Flávio que vive en Estados Unidos, dijo antes de las elecciones que una derrota electoral le obligaría a marcharse del país. "Si mi hermano no gana, estoy a favor de que se marche del país", dijo al podcaster Steven Crowder el 23 de octubre.

item.title: Canada, UAE sign trade deal as Carney seeks new trading partners
item.description: Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a comprehensive trade deal on Tuesday to lower barriers between the two economies and boost investment, the governments said, as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to expand trade and investment ties at a time of tension with the United States.
item.dc:creator: Promit Mukherjee, Federico Maccioni
item.content:encoded: Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a comprehensive trade deal on Tuesday to lower barriers between the two economies and boost investment, the governments said, as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to expand trade and investment ties at a time of tension with the United States. Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan presided over the signing of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), which aims to cut tariffs, reduce red tape and improve market access for businesses in both countries. Carney has vowed to double Canada's non-US trade over the next decade as President Donald Trump's tariffs have rippled through Canada's economy. Subsequent attempts for a deal with Washington have broken down, and that has pushed Carney to aggressively pursue trade pacts with countries from the Asia Pacific to Europe and Middle East. "Once fully implemented, the CEPA will reduce or eliminate tariffs on over 99% of current Canadian exports to the UAE. That means new markets for Canadian farmers growing pulses and canola, for manufacturers of industrial machinery and power generation equipment, for our world-class aerospace sector, and other Canadian innovators," The Prime Minister's Office said in a statement. "The agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment, and expand market access for Canadian goods and services, including in the industrial, agricultural, forest, fish and seafood, environmental, and engineering sectors," it said, adding CEPA is expected to enter into force in 2027. The two countries also signed preliminary agreements on energy, diplomatic and defence cooperation. "We see considerable potential for our private sector, whether through improved market access for our exporters or access to investment opportunities in high-growth sectors such as logistics, communications, advanced technology and manufacturing – all of which will support our pursuit of a resilient, diversified and globally connected economy,” UAE's Foreign Trade Minister Thani Al Zeyoudi said in a statement. He signed the CEPA deal with his Canadian counterpart Maninder Sidhu. UAE is the largest Middle Eastern market for Canadian exports and is a big buyer of Canadian motor vehicles and parts, and machinery. Two-way trade between the countries was worth C$3.5 billion ($2.48 billion) last year. It has been growing at 10% annually for the last few years, according to a government data. The UAE last year also committed up to in Canada. The signing is the last step before Canada’s Parliament can ratify the agreement, a Canadian government source said.

item.title: Monedas cierran mixtas, real brasileño se recupera tras desplome en la jornada previa
item.description: Las monedas de América Latina anotaron un desempeño dispar el martes, en una jornada en que el real brasileño se recuperó de parte del desplome de la ronda previa, mientras la atención del mercado se centraba en el inicio de la reunión de política monetaria de la Reserva Federal de Estados Unidos.
item.dc:creator: Froilan Romero
item.content:encoded: Las monedas de América Latina anotaron un desempeño dispar el martes, en una jornada en que el real brasileño se recuperó de parte del desplome de la ronda previa, mientras la atención del mercado se centraba en el inicio de la reunión de política monetaria de la Reserva Federal de Estados Unidos. * Los activos brasileños se hundieron el lunes debido al triunfo del presidente de izquierda Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva en el balotaje ante Flávio Bolsonaro, favorito de los mercados. * La Fed mantendría sin cambios las tasas de interés el miércoles, y el mercado espera pistas sobre si podría haber un alza en diciembre. Según la herramienta FedWatch de CME, los operadores ven una probabilidad del 80% de un aumento de tipos a fines de año. * El real brasileño se apreció un 1,07%, a 5,3488 unidades por dólar tras hundirse más de un 8% el lunes. En tanto, el índice Bovespa (.BVSP) de la bolsa B3 de Sao Paulo bajó un 0,44%, a 175.831,92 puntos, luego que el lunes anotó su mayor caída diaria desde marzo de 2020. * El peso mexicano cotizaba cerca del cierre en 18,6743 unidades por dólar, con una caída del 0,59%.
