item.title: United Parcel Service expects fatter holiday profits on slightly slimmer volume
item.description: United Parcel Service's focus on more lucrative business means it can make more money delivering slightly fewer packages during its critical peak holiday season and every year going forward, CEO Carol Tome said on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Nandan Mandayam, Lisa Baertlein
item.content:encoded: United Parcel Service's focus on more lucrative business means it can make more money delivering slightly fewer packages during its critical peak holiday season and every year going forward, CEO Carol Tome said on Tuesday. Shares of the world's largest parcel delivery firm closed almost 6% higher after UPS (UPS.N) raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts on better-than-expected third-quarter earnings after cutting doorstep deliveries of millions of unprofitable packages for Amazon.com (AMZN.O) , its largest customer. Atlanta-based UPS expects total average daily volume to be down 1.3% in the fourth quarter as it becomes more selective in which packages it delivers. At the same time, executives forecast a roughly 3% rise in revenue in the company's domestic operation, its largest, and an estimated 7% increase in international revenue. "We're dispelling the old belief that all packages were created equal and that volume solves all problems," Tome told Reuters. A widening gap between the cost per parcel and revenue per parcel will improve company margins, executives said. For example, UPS' reduction in unprofitable deliveries — and the resulting volume reduction — in the fourth quarter means UPS can spend less on labor as well as truck and plane leases to handle the holiday package surge, Chief Financial Officer Brian Dykes said. Tome said the outlook for the holiday season, referred to as the Super Bowl for delivery firms and retailers, is strong as US consumers continue spending despite pressures from rising inflation and prices at the pump. SLIMMER OPERATION SETS STAGE FOR GROWTH UPS has shuttered facilities and shed thousands of jobs after scaling back deliveries for Amazon. UPS said it completed the Amazon delivery reductions in the second quarter. Rival FedEx (FDX.N) , which reports results on Wednesday, has deployed a similar strategy. Both companies have been under pressure from investors to show meaningful results. Tome also said [USN:L6N46C12E TEXT:"data center"] construction is a significant opportunity as it touches every part of UPS, which can fly in critical components such as microprocessors, arrange ocean shipments of equipment, store goods and make final deliveries. For the third quarter, UPS posted adjusted profit of $1.69 per share, lower than $1.74 per share a year ago but above analysts' average estimate of $1.63. Third-quarter adjusted operating margin in UPS' domestic unit, which generates about 65% of company revenue, rose to 7% from 6.4% a year earlier. The smaller but more profitable international package division also reported a higher adjusted operating margin of 14.9% for the third quarter, compared with 14.8% last year. Jefferies analysts said third-quarter earnings showcased a "quarter of strong execution," while Evercore ISI analyst Jonathan Chappell wrote in a note that the results give "some confidence in durability." UPS also said it was on track to meet its target of $3 billion in cost savings this year. It has saved $1.8 billion through September. The company now expects 2026 adjusted profit of around $7.28 per share, compared with the $7.22 it had forecast in July. Analysts expect the company to report a profit of $7.19 per share, according to data compiled by LSEG. UPS expects annual revenue of $92.6 billion, compared with its previous projection of $91.2 billion and above analysts' estimate of $91.73 billion.

item.title: Fashion's AI era: face swaps and digital clones
item.description: AI-generated fashion models present a tantalizing opportunity for brands: the ability to create lifelike images for their retail websites while cutting costs by 90% or more compared to photo shoots with human models.
item.dc:creator: Helen Reid
item.content:encoded: AI-generated fashion models present a tantalizing opportunity for brands: the ability to create lifelike images for their retail websites while cutting costs by 90% or more compared to photo shoots with human models. For the modeling industry, the technology poses an existential threat because of scant regulation governing the ownership or use of digital twins. Fashion models face the risk of unpaid replication of their image – or replacement by entirely synthetic models. To understand how AI is upending the economics of fashion modeling, Reuters interviewed 15 model-agency directors and reviewed more than a dozen confidential photo-shoot contracts in which brands including Diesel, Calvin Klein and L'Oreal (OREP.PA) detailed proposed terms for AI-created alterations and future use of the images. The companies’ contract requests included the right to swap a model's face with another using AI; the creation of a digital clone with no additional compensation to the model; and the right to use images of a model's body to train AI. The terms in the unsigned contracts also included broad legal language that could effectively give a brand leeway to use AI however it wanted. While some companies are looking to repurpose or modify images of existing models, others are using fully AI-generated models, not based on existing humans. As AI use expands, modeling agencies are seeing bookings decline, photo studios are closing and models are facing the loss of a chunk of their livelihoods: photo shoots by fast-fashion retailers constantly adding new collections to their websites. "Within a year, even the next six months, there's going to be less jobs for models, especially our bread and butter, which is ecommerce," said Adot Gak, a model based in London who has been on the cover of Harper's Bazaar and appeared in campaigns by brands including Balmain and H&M. "If we don't speak up about this, in the next two years the whole industry will just be bots." While some fast-fashion players like Spain’s Mango have already rolled out AI-generated models at scale, high-end brands are moving more cautiously. Moncler experimented early with an AI-generated campaign in 2023, and Gucci caused controversy in fashion circles when it posted images generated by AI on Instagram this year. Moncler said it does not currently use AI-generated models, either on its website or in its campaigns. Gucci did not respond to requests for comment. "The scariest part is that now people cannot differentiate between a real model and an AI model," said Gak. FACE SWAPS AND 'DIGITAL TWINS' AI allows retailers to endlessly rework and redeploy a model’s image wearing different outfits at a fraction of the cost of new shoots. "Some brands ask to modify faces, bodies, skin, age or expressions after shoots using AI. Others are asking about creating 'digital twins' of models that they can reuse later without needing another production," said Patrick Staal, owner of modeling agency Uniko Models in Barcelona. In a photo-shoot casting sheet, Italian brand Diesel asked models to agree to "alteration or reconstruction of facial features and body proportions,” along with “swapping of faces among the participating models,” and “superimposition of the Participant’s face onto another person’s body.” Diesel's parent company OTB told Reuters the model release was drafted for a specific campaign and isn’t representative of its typical agreements. It said it doesn’t systematically modify models with AI. Reale Actives – the skincare brand launched this year by social-media personality Alix Earle – uses the tagline, "Reale you is perfect you." But in a contract seen by Reuters, the brand asked for rights to create AI-generated replicas of models and to "own" and use these fakes for a year without further compensation. Reale Actives said in a statement that it uses real models and hasn’t replicated any model using AI. It said the contract language came from a partner production company, which it declined to name. MODELS TRAINING THEIR MACHINE REPLACEMENTS? In some cases, models are helping to train their replacements: some contracts’ fine print includes language allowing the use of their images to train AI tools. A Calvin Klein draft contract seen by Reuters asked the model to accept, for no extra pay, that the brand “may use reasonably unrecognizable images of Model (no identifying features such as Model's face, scars, tattoos or otherwise) to train and fine tune AI tools for learning general model attributes.” A Calvin Klein spokesperson said in a statement: "Like many others, we are testing and learning in this fast-moving space," adding that the brand's AI use is guided by regulation, industry standards and respect for models' rights. In many cases, contracts include wording such as "including" or "not limited to," which lawyers commonly use to claim rights that aren’t spelled out. Melanie Howard, partner and chair of luxury brands at law firm Loeb & Loeb in Los Angeles, represents both brands and talent in contract negotiations and said such sweeping language "is dangerous in its ambiguity” and makes it difficult for models to challenge any unsanctioned use of their images. In a photo-shoot contract seen by Reuters, France’s L'Oreal asked for "the right to use artificial intelligence (AI) technologies... including for the purpose of modifying, enhancing, or adapting the appearance of cosmetic products, packaging, or shades, as well as for retouching purposes." Without addressing that contract language, L'Oreal said it uses standard AI tools in post-production and editing that don't affect the model's image. 'WE ARE SAVING SO MUCH MONEY' Some firms are openly embracing AI to replace models and save money. Europe's biggest online-fashion retailer, Zalando, has rapidly [USN:L8N3RE3M7 TEXT:"adopted AI-generated imagery"] for marketing content – and shut both its photo studios in Berlin last year. Fast-fashion retailer About You, which Zalando acquired in July last year, also closed its studio. Overall, Zalando cut more than 340 jobs, though the company said it retained some of those employees in other roles. Now, About You is launching its Scayle Studios business, which creates digital imagery for other retailers using AI-generated models and promises a more than 90% production-cost reduction. Scayle has 130 brand clients and has generated 190,000 outfits in the last month, according to a company spokesperson. "We are saving so much money," said Julian Jansen, vice president of marketing at About You. "You've always had this super fast world of ecommerce, and this super slow traditional world of photo shoots, it didn't fit together in any way – and now with AI, it's a completely different scale." LITTLE REGULATION Regulations globally haven’t kept pace with the threat to models’ livelihoods, but the New York State Fashion Workers Act is one exception. The law has made it illegal since June 2025 for brands to create or modify replicas of models without their explicit consent. "The misuse of models' images is not new, but with AI that problem is accelerated tenfold," said Sara Ziff, founder and executive director of the New York-based nonprofit Model Alliance, which backed the legislation. Ziff, herself a model for years, pushes for similar laws in other states and federally. The British Fashion Model Agents Association has drawn up an AI code of practice, including that AI can only be used with the consent of a model, who would own any digital twin. But BFMA head John Horner said that without binding regulation in Britain or Europe, models still risk being taken advantage of by less scrupulous agents. "A lot of young talents don’t fully understand the long-term consequences yet," said Staal, the Barcelona-based model agency director. "Signing away AI rights at 20 years old could still affect someone ten years later."

item.title: Last Republican incumbent senator in a Democratic-leaning state fights for survival
item.description: If Republican Senator Susan Collins wins this nail-biter of an election, it may well be because voters in Maine decide she is not Republican enough.
item.dc:creator: Andy Sullivan
item.content:encoded: If Republican Senator Susan Collins wins this nail-biter of an election, it may well be because voters in Maine decide she is not Republican enough. Since her first victory in 1996, Collins’ reputation as an independent-minded moderate has helped her win reelection even as Maine backed Democrats for president. Now the only Republican incumbent running in a Democratic-leaning state, she is deadlocked in opinion polls with Democrat Troy Jackson in a race that could help determine control of the US Senate. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the 100-seat Senate from Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections . Jackson, a rough-hewn former logger and state Senate president, has attacked Collins as a rubber stamp for Republican President Donald Trump . Collins is countering with the clout she has amassed over her 30-year Senate career, highlighting projects she has funded and carve-outs she has secured to lessen the [USN:L1N4680R7 TEXT:"economic fallout"] from Trump’s spending cuts, tariffs and war with Iran. “If it wasn't Susan Collins, this race would have been over three months ago,” said Maine Democratic consultant Toby McGrath. But strategists in both parties say the pool of the independent-minded, persuadable voters who backed Collins in previous elections has shrunk as partisan lines have hardened and Trump has galvanized Democrats in opposition. “If you hate Trump, you're voting for whoever the Democrats put on the ballot,” said Phil Harriman, a former Republican state senator. Democrats faced a potential debacle this summer, when Graham Platner, an oyster farmer and Marine veteran, won the party’s nomination [USN:S0N42B09J TEXT:"only to drop out"] after facing a rape accusation that he denied. The party quickly united behind Jackson, who has invoked his hardscrabble upbringing in the remote logging town of Allagash as he campaigns on a populist agenda of universal healthcare and raising taxes on the wealthy. “I saw at a young age how people with money and power and influence can hold people back,” he said at a campaign event on Saturday. $1.5 BILLION IN EARMARKS In recent weeks, Collins has visited projects she has funded through her work on the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee: a wastewater treatment plant in North Windham, a dock in Bucksport, an emergency center in Farmington. She says she has secured nearly $1.5 billion in earmarks since 2021. “This has required hard work, knowledge and seniority. The question for voters in this campaign is who can do more for Maine,” she said at an October 15 debate. That influence, she argues, has also helped to shield Maine from the Trump administration’s policies. As Trump’s [USN:L6N4580Y1 TEXT:"trade war with Canada"] has hammered the state’s economy, Collins has pointed to tariff exemptions the administration has granted at her request for road salt, cement and equipment used by the state’s blueberry, potato and apple growers. The Trump administration also credited her when it released home-heating oil reserves to try to drive down prices that have increased more than 70% since last year – a [USN:L6N461155 TEXT:"crucial issue"] in a state where roughly half of households rely on the product. Collins has also pointed to a $50 billion fund she crafted to help [USN:L6N3S70P7 TEXT:"rural hospitals"] cope with healthcare cuts in the 2025 tax and spending package that enacted most of Trump’s legislative agenda, as well as money for body-worn cameras and de-escalation training for federal immigration agents following the January killing of two US citizens in Minnesota. 'THERE SHOULDN'T BE A LIST' Jackson argues that these carve-outs amount to little when weighed against the damage caused by Trump. Body cameras and de-escalation training did not stop an immigration agent from [USN:L6N43H0SA TEXT:"killing a state resident"] in July, he says, and residents would not be struggling to heat their homes if Trump had not started the war with Iran, which has pushed up oil prices globally. Trump’s trade war with Canada, he argues, is only possible because Republicans in Congress have surrendered their authority over tariffs to Trump. “I can't believe that the most powerful US senator in the world would stand there and say, 'Well, I got this and this and that off the list,' instead of the fact that there shouldn’t be a list,” he said on Saturday. SIX ADS IN A ROW Meanwhile, a relentless ad war has played out over the state’s airwaves. AdImpact, an analysis firm, estimates $199 million will be spent on the race – equal to $170 for every adult in the state. During a local newscast on Friday, six ads in a row were devoted to the contest. Those ads are chasing a small slice of undecided voters. Democratic activists say they are encountering relatively few people who have yet to decide on a candidate as they campaign door-to-door in Windham, a Portland suburb that backed Collins by a 14-point margin in 2020, even as it backed Democrat Joe Biden over Trump for president. “There’s just a lot less of that persuadable middle than we historically see,” said volunteer Austin Coco. Windham resident Jim Tabor, a retired optician, said he has grown disillusioned with the Republican Party under Trump. A Collins supporter in past elections, he said this year he will back Jackson. “If he turns out to be a bum, I’ll vote against him next time. But Susan Collins won’t be there,” he said.

item.title: Crypto blitzes midterms with $176 million to support allies as it prepares for post-Trump era
item.description: The crypto industry has spent roughly $176 million across more than 100 midterm races this election cycle, as part of a years-long plan to build a bipartisan coalition of allies in Congress that can advance its interests long after US President Donald Trump leaves office.
item.dc:creator: Dawn Kopecki
item.content:encoded: The crypto industry has spent roughly $176 million across more than 100 midterm races this election cycle, as part of a years-long plan to build a bipartisan coalition of allies in Congress that can advance its interests long after US President Donald Trump leaves office. The $2.75 trillion industry, and the billionaires who built it, are aggressively spending to elect friendly candidates while targeting politicians they see as a threat, according to interviews with more than a half-dozen crypto political strategists and a Reuters review of the spending. While the industry’s recent spending blitz is known, its long-term plan to further its legislative agenda is less well-understood. The industry isn’t just looking for allies; it is trying to pick candidates who already have a chance of winning, and can help once they get to Congress, the strategists said. Crypto's largest super political action committee, Fairshake, which spent $196 million during the 2024 election cycle, is leading the industry’s strategy again. Fairshake said 53 of the 58 candidates it supported in primaries or special elections this year won and will be on the ballot on November 3. Super PACs can accept and spend unlimited sums of money, but cannot coordinate directly with campaigns. They are flooding several races with tens of millions of dollars in ads. Voters have little way of knowing who pays for these ads, which barely mention crypto. Most of Fairshake's are sponsored by its affiliate PACs with innocuous names like "Defend American Jobs" and "Protect Progress." The ads often focus on hot-button issues like taxes or immigration. Perceived enemies, such as longtime skeptic Sherrod Brown, vying to return to the Senate in Ohio, can be subjected to an onslaught of often-personal attacks. Advocacy group Public Citizen said crypto was the single-biggest corporate spender in federal races in 2026, after saying in 2024 that its spending was "akin to a corporate Death Star hovering over elections." The PACs' primary financiers, led by Coinbase, Ripple and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, aren't trying to convince voters to support digital currencies. The money is a calling card to help forge long-term relationships with elected officials, said industry strategists, campaign staff, watchdog groups and political finance managers. It underscores how the industry is behaving as other businesses do in Washington — using funds to open doors and buffer itself against regulation. The strategy reflects the reality that come 2029, the occupant of the White House is unlikely to be as personally invested in crypto as Trump, whose family made around $2.3 billion from crypto ventures between mid-2024 and April, a Reuters investigation found . “It's an investment in the future,” said Colin McLaren, head of government relations at crypto industry advocacy group the Solana Policy Institute, which has given $4.9 million to the midterms this year, according to campaign finance records. The effort is designed to “ensure that over the next 100 years, the crypto industry has clear rules of the road, and that we know what our regulators are expecting from us," he said. Through October 20, Fairshake and its affiliate PACs have spent about $150.8 million on the midterms this year, while other crypto groups have spent around $25 million, according to campaign finance filings. "We back pro-crypto candidates who support American innovation in both parties, and look forward to continuing to build on the largest pro-crypto caucus in American history," said Geoff Vetter, spokesperson for Fairshake. COME A LONG WAY In 2018, lawmakers couldn’t even get a room in the House or Senate office buildings to hold the first congressional bipartisan roundtable discussion on crypto, instead meeting across the street from the US Capitol in the Library of Congress, said Kristin Smith, president of the Solana Policy Institute, who helped establish the Blockchain Association that year. The Biden administration heavily scrutinized the industry following the collapse of FTX and an [USN:L3N2X40RX TEXT:"industry-wide meltdown"] in 2022, with the US Securities and Exchange Commission eventually levying more than $6 billion in penalties in 98 cases, according to a Georgetown University Law study. “It was an all-out assault on the technology,” said Smith, the Blockchain Association's interim CEO. “The industry was in a corner, and the only way out was to show political force.” Executives decided they needed a political strategy to combat what they called then-SEC chair Gary Gensler’s “regulation by enforcement,” lobbyists, advocacy groups and campaign strategists said. Coinbase Chief Policy Officer Faryar Shirzad was the architect behind nonprofit political advocacy group Stand With Crypto — which isn't required to disclose its donors — and Fairshake, which both launched in 2023. The number of Congresspeople with an "A" rating from Stand With Crypto is up to 332, compared with 96 when the group launched. As the industry has won more legal clarity in Washington, its market value has nearly tripled from around $1 trillion in 2023 to about $2.75 trillion now, according to CoinGecko . The combination of Trump, a growing bipartisan congressional coalition and a neutered opposition allowed the industry to advance its legislative agenda more in the last two years than some industries have done in decades, other industry lobbyists say. That includes 2025's Genius Act legislation establishing the first-ever US federal regulatory framework for stablecoins, enacted with overwhelming bipartisan support. That followed a White House meeting earlier in the year when industry leaders, including Coinbase (COIN.O) CEO Brian Armstrong and Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse, [USN:L2N3PP0UZ TEXT:"sat with Trump"] when the president declared an end to the "war on crypto." "Moving that quickly in Washington is like light speed in space," said Ron Bonjean, partner at bipartisan public affairs firm Rokk Solutions, and a former senior Senate aide. The industry's real goal is passing the Clarity Act, which would put crypto oversight under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. That bill stalled in this congressional session and faces an uphill battle next year if Democrats win control of one or more chambers of Congress. Without it, agency-level [USN:FWN45Q05G TEXT:"regulations undertaken during Trump's term"] can be reversed by a subsequent administration, analysts at JPMorgan said. Fairshake is financing House candidates from both parties, but it decided to only back Republicans in Senate races after Democrats in that chamber blocked the Clarity Act from advancing to a final vote. Their opposition centered around an ethics provision that would have forced the Trump family to sell their crypto holdings. Gary Kalman, of anti-corruption nonprofit Transparency International, criticized the bill for shifting regulation to the less-stringent CFTC, and for preempting states from enacting tougher laws. Coinbase and Andreessen Horowitz declined to comment. Ripple didn't return requests for comment. THE PRIME TARGET Fairshake's highest-profile win in 2024 was defeating Brown, an industry foe who chaired the Senate Banking Committee from 2021 to 2024. Spending millions attacking the sitting chairman of the industry's oversight committee was unprecedented in Washington, corporate watchdogs and political strategists say. But the gamble paid off. Now, Brown is running again, with public opinion polls showing him with a narrow lead over his opponent, Republican Jon Husted. The industry has spent more than $68 million on the race, helping to make it one of the most expensive on record, according to AdImpact. Fairshake’s ads opposing Brown, which it did not comment on, don't mention crypto. One charges him with voting to raise gas taxes in Ohio and raises a [USN:L1N2ZT27M TEXT:"Reuters-debunked claim"] that he voted to "unleash 87,000 IRS agents on you while voting to give social security benefits to illegals." “Of course, the special interests are panicking, they know Sherrod will fight the rigged system they're feasting on to stand up for working Ohioans,” said Patrick Eisenhauer, Brown's campaign manager. A CRYPTO MONEY BOMB In some races, crypto spending dwarfed candidate fundraising. The industry spent $5.3 million in a Maryland House Democratic primary to support state Delegate Adrian Boafo, who raised $1.9 million on his own, records show. Other non-crypto groups spent $6.8 million to support Boafo's campaign, which declined to comment. “There were so many ads ... that it makes other candidates suffocate,” said Quincy Bareebe, a healthcare entrepreneur who came in second of 24 candidates in that primary despite spending $6.6 million of her own money. "Adrian was everywhere." The industry was less successful in Illinois. Fairshake spent over $10.1 million on ads attacking [USN:L1N4001C8 TEXT:"Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton"], who is running for US Senate, and another $2.5 million against Illinois state Representative La Shawn Ford, who is running for a Chicago-area congressional district. Both are expected to win on November 3. Ford defeated a dozen primary challengers despite raising just $500,000 and lending his campaign $175,000 to fight off industry-funded ads that brought up a 14-year-old federal indictment that was later dropped. His campaign issued a cease-and-desist letter to Fairshake, accusing it of making defamatory statements about him in its ads. Fairshake did not comment on its ads or Ford's response. Ford thinks Fairshake targeted him because he supported state legislation to require crypto exchanges and related companies to register with Illinois. “They were relentless, on every outlet, radio, TV, social media, mailers," Ford said. “It was personal and it was hurtful, and unnecessary for my family to have to go through.”

item.title: Wall Street ends higher on revived AI momentum
item.description: An AI-fueled tech rally sent US stocks to a higher close on Tuesday as third-quarter reporting season gained steam, while the Federal Reserve convened for its penultimate meeting of the year.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Culp, Shashwat Chauhan
item.content:encoded: An AI-fueled tech rally sent US stocks to a higher close on Tuesday as third-quarter reporting season gained steam, while the Federal Reserve convened for its penultimate meeting of the year. The tech-heavy Nasdaq led the gains. The buzz surrounding [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"details"] of Anthropic's impending initial public offering helped boost chip stocks (.SOX) for the third consecutive session. Growing concerns over the viability of debt-funded spending amid rising borrowing costs have weighed on the AI trade this month. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index, while off more than 20% from its June 22 record closing high, has outperformed the broader market this year, gaining 62.1% compared with the S&P 500's 12.8% year-to-date advance. To fund its AI expansion, [USN:L3N46C0RT TEXT:"Meta"] (META.O) increased its largest-ever equity fundraising to $97.5 billion, sending the Facebook parent's shares down 1.6%. "(The Anthropic news) seems to be giving a little bit of a relief rally to the AI stocks, particularly the semis," said Chuck Carlson, CEO at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana, referring to chip stocks. "Those stocks have gotten clobbered in recent weeks and they were probably due for a bounce." [USN:L2N46D0L0 TEXT:"Economic data"] showed rising new orders for computers and peripheral equipment, supporting the notion of strong AI-related spending. Nearly half of S&P 500 companies have reported third-quarter results. Of those, 83% have delivered better-than-expected results, according to the most recent available LSEG data. [USN:L3N46D14Q TEXT:"Boeing"] (BA.N) tumbled 10.7% following its bigger-than-expected third-quarter loss, while water-management company [USN:L2N46D0E8 TEXT:"Xylem"] (XYL.N) slid 14.2% after trimming full-year forecasts. [USN:L3N46D0V7 TEXT:"United Parcel Service"] (UPS.N) advanced 5.8% after the package delivery firm raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts. [USN:L3N46D14Q TEXT:"Sherwin-Williams"]' (SHW.N) quarterly profit miss sent the stock 2.7% lower, weighing on the Dow. [USN:L2N46D0CZ TEXT:"Royal Caribbean"] (RCL.N) rose 5.5% after the cruise operator lifted its full-year profit forecast. Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Alphabet (GOOGL.O) results are expected on Wednesday, while Amazon.com is due to report on Thursday. The Fed convened on Tuesday for its October monetary policy meeting, which is widely expected to culminate in a decision to keep the fed funds target rate on hold in the 3.75% to 4% range, saving its second rate hike of the year for its final meeting in December, according to CME's FedWatch tool. "There seems to be more confidence that the Fed isn't going to do anything at this meeting, partly because we have an election on Tuesday," Carlson added. "There's probably at least some relief that the rate situation is not going to get in the way of a rally." The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 15.99 points, or 0.03%, to 52,377.57, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 45.83 points, or 0.60%, to 7,722.60 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 308.43 points, or 1.18%, to 26,477.81. Of the 11 major sectors in the S&P 500, technology led the gainers, while energy shares suffered the steepest percentage decline, hit by easing [USN:L2N46D0E8 TEXT:"crude prices"] as attention turned to Middle East peace negotiations. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.83-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 81 new highs and 146 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 3,118 stocks rose and 1,680 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.86-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 11 new 52-week highs and six new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 62 new highs and 239 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 16.10 billion shares, compared with the 17.18 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

item.title: Football Accusé d'avoir offensé la Chine, Mbappé s'excuse mais perd plusieurs partenaires chinois
item.description: Kylian Mbappé, lâché par plusieurs entreprises chinoises après des propos polémiques sur le "dictateur" Mao Zedong, a tenté mardi d'éteindre l'incendie en présentant ses excuses et en marquant son "profond respect pour le peuple chinois et son histoire".
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Kylian Mbappé, lâché par plusieurs entreprises chinoises après des propos polémiques sur le "dictateur" Mao Zedong, a tenté mardi d'éteindre l'incendie en présentant ses excuses et en marquant son "profond respect pour le peuple chinois et son histoire". Dans une vidéo apparue en ligne lundi, on entend l'international français expliquer que le "mème" - une image ou une vidéo, souvent parodique, reprise massivement sur internet - le plus drôle qu'il ait vu de lui-même était celui où son visage avait été greffé sur celui d'"un dictateur chinois". A savoir l'ancien dirigeant chinois Mao Zedong. Les fans multiplient les mèmes superposant le visage du Madrilène à ceux de dirigeants militaires et politiques, suggérant son supposé autoritarisme. Fondateur de la République populaire de Chine, Mao Zedong est perçu par nombre de Chinois comme le sauveur de la nation et les plaisanteries à son sujet sont considérées comme un tabou. Il est mort en 1976. "Lors d'une récente interview, j'ai réagi à une image de moi me mettant en scène. Ce propos était maladroit, et je comprends aujourd'hui qu'il a blessé de nombreuses personnes en Chine et au sein de la communauté chinoise à travers le monde", déclare l'attaquant du Real Madrid dans un communiqué en français, chinois, et anglais. "Je présente mes excuses à toutes celles et ceux que mes mots ont heurtés. Ce n'était absolument pas mon intention. J'ai un profond respect pour le peuple chinois et son histoire, et je suis sincèrement désolé", ajoute-t-il. Dans un entretien accordé le mois dernier à L'Équipe, le Tricolore avait estimé que si certains aspects de cette tendance relevaient du simple divertissement, les mèmes viraux le présentant en dictateur traduisaient "un manque de conscience politique et humaine chez les gens". La controverse autour de la figure de Mao Zedong a pris une telle ampleur que plusieurs partenaires chinois du sportif ont manifesté leur réprobation en rompant avec lui. Ainsi Eastroc Beverage, qui utilisait l'image de Kylian Mbappé sur ses boissons, a déclaré sur le réseau social chinois Weibo s'opposer fermement à tout "comportement qui heurte les sentiments nationaux". "À compter de ce jour, nous mettons fin à toute coopération avec Kylian Mbappé", a ajouté la marque, avant le communiqué d'excuses du footballeur. Les groupes laitiers Mengniu et Milkground ont eux aussi mis fin à leur partenariat avec l'attaquant français. "MALAISE ET OFFENSE" Interrogé sur l'affaire, un porte-parole du ministère chinois des Affaires étrangères a indiqué que les paroles et actes portant atteinte aux sentiments du peuple chinois "se heurteront naturellement à un rejet commun de l'ensemble de la société". La télévision d'État chinoise a suspendu la diffusion de tous les matches et événements impliquant la Liga et Kylian Mbappé. Les publicités dans lesquelles apparaît le joueur ont également été retirées, a rapporté mardi The Paper, un média public chinois. "De la part de la Liga, nous regrettons profondément les déclarations de Kylian Mbappé qui ont provoqué malaise et offense en Chine. Nous comprenons le tort causé et, au nom de la Liga, je souhaite présenter nos sincères excuses au peuple chinois", a déclaré Javier Tebas, le président de la Liga, sur le réseau social X. Ce dernier a ensuite annoncé s'être entretenu avec l'ambassadeur chinois en Espagne pour "trouver des solutions permettant de surmonter cet épisode". "Notre engagement est de continuer à travailler ensemble pour qu'un épisode individuel ne mette pas en péril les avancées importantes effectuées et ne touche pas les millions de fans chinois qui suivent nos compétitions", a déclaré Javier Tebas dans un communiqué publié sur les réseaux sociaux. "La Chine est et restera un partenaire stratégique pour la Liga." La chaîne de télévision publique CCTV a déclaré qu'elle écouterait ce que Kylian Mbappé a à dire après ses excuses et, "plus important encore", observerait ce qu'il ferait. "Nous espérons que la Liga, le Real Madrid et Mbappé lui-même tireront véritablement les leçons de cet épisode, présenteront des excuses sincères et corrigeront en profondeur leurs erreurs", a-t-elle indiqué dans un communiqué. La marque suisse On, dont il est l'ambassadeur depuis le mois dernier, a dit "[prendre] acte avec satisfaction des excuses de Kylian Mbappé". "Nous avons un profond respect pour le peuple chinois et le riche patrimoine culturel de la Chine. Nous restons en dialogue avec nos partenaires et n'avons pas d'autre commentaire à faire pour le moment", a-t-elle ajouté.

item.title: Two Nordic leaders urge Putin to end Ukraine war in rare direct contact by Europeans
item.description: The leaders of Finland and Norway phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine, breaking with a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin.
item.dc:creator: Essi Lehto
item.content:encoded: The leaders of Finland and Norway phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine , breaking with a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin. The call by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was an attempt to influence the diplomatic process after US President Donald Trump shifted his position in favour of Russia and US ties with Ukraine hit their lowest point in 18 months. Stoere said he and Stubb had spoken to Putin for about 90 minutes, and then to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. In a joint statement, they linked the initiative to planned peace discussions between Russian, Ukrainian and US officials in Abu Dhabi next month, their first since February. Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on how to end the war that began with Russia's invasion in February 2022, and long-range airstrikes by both sides have increased this year while battle lines have remained largely static. "The discussion (with Putin) was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said. Stoere said he and Stubb had "stressed the importance of de-escalation." Both voiced strong support for Ukraine. In later comments to Finnish journalists, Stubb said all Western allies were consulted on the initiative, adding that Ukraine had sought the opening of a new communications channel and Europe could no longer be a bystander to peace efforts giving Russia "the silent treatment". NO SIGN OF KREMLIN COMPROMISE The Kremlin's readout of the call did not suggest any softening of Putin's position. "It was emphasised that achieving a just and long-term peace is possible only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account," it said. "At the same time, attention was drawn to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are contributing to the prolongation of the hostilities." Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Tuesday's call had offered nothing new on the Ukraine conflict, with an information war likely to escalate, and that European countries were simply seeking a role in the negotiation process. Western European leaders have mostly refused to talk to Putin, hoping to isolate him. But they have been sidelined in peace efforts led by US President Donald Trump, who is seen in many European capitals as unpredictable and prone to side with Putin at Ukraine's expense. That perception has been reinforced by deals this month in which Putin agreed to supply Russian diesel to the United States and Trump eased sanctions on Russia. Ukraine has also complained of disruption to intelligence-sharing by the US and to satellite internet services on which its military relies. Gerhard Mangott, an Austrian political analyst, said European governments had "manoeuvred themselves into a dead end" when it came to finding a solution to the war, and Tuesday's call was an effort to establish a channel for dialogue. He drew attention to remarks by Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov on Sunday suggesting [USN:L2N46B01R TEXT:"Europe should be part of discussions"]. "I interpret this as a shift in Russia's position, given that Moscow had previously consistently rejected the idea of discussing a settlement of the war in Ukraine with the Europeans," Mangott said. DANISH LEADER'S CRITICISM Ukrainian Foreign Minister [USN:S8N44Z03H TEXT:"Andrii Sybiha"] said the call had been coordinated with Kyiv and was "the right approach". "We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and peace process," he said, adding that he also hoped a local ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of [USN:L2N46D011 TEXT:"Oleshky"] could "pave the way to other steps in the peace process." But Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she saw no signs that Russia wanted peace, adding: "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo." Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said other European leaders were not informed of the talks. "My impression is that everyone wants peace, except for Putin himself. I have quite low expectations for this type of conversation," Kristersson told Swedish daily DN. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had told Stubb and Stoere that "absolute caution and vigilance are necessary in such contacts". Stubb and Stoere said they acted as leaders of their respective countries and not on behalf of Europe, and had "consulted thoroughly with all our partners." Russia has frequently accused European governments of stoking the war by arming Ukraine and refusing direct talks. A source close to the Kremlin said French President Emmanuel Macron had been the last EU leader to speak with Putin — in a summer call that yielded no results and was not made public. The source said Putin told Stubb and Stoere that the European involvement was welcome and that the war needed to end "taking into account the realities on the ground". Asked what this meant, the person said it signified that Russia would not compromise over its aim to capture the whole of Ukraine's Donbas region. The Europeans responded by saying a "just" peace was needed, the source said.

item.title: Mbappe seeks to defuse anger in China after Mao 'dictator' comment
item.description: France soccer captain Kylian Mbappe apologised to China on Tuesday after a fierce backlash over his comments referring to late Chinese leader Mao Zedong as a dictator, underscoring how swiftly global celebrities can come unstuck.
item.dc:creator: Casey Hall, Clare Jim
item.content:encoded: France soccer captain Kylian Mbappe apologised to China on Tuesday after a fierce backlash over his comments referring to late Chinese leader Mao Zedong as a dictator, underscoring how swiftly global celebrities can come unstuck. In a video on a French podcast that has since been taken down, Mbappe is heard discussing a funny meme where his face had been photoshopped on to that of "some guy — I think he's a Chinese dictator". "During a recent interview, I reacted to an image of myself," Real Madrid forward Mbappe said in a statement. "My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. "I apologise to everyone my words have upset," added Mbappe, who has ties with firms including Swiss sportswear brand On Holding (49G.BN) , hotel chain Accor (ACCP.PA) and Lego. "This was absolutely not my intention." The backlash highlighted the risks for athletes and brands in the lucrative China market, where satire about Mao, modern China's founding leader who ruled the country from 1949 until his death in 1976, remains a social taboo. LaLiga President Javier Tebas said that he held a meeting with the ambassador of China in Spain to address the situation and "seek solutions that allow us to overcome this episode." "Our commitment is to keep working together so that an individual episode does not harm the important advances achieved nor affect the millions of Chinese fans who follow our competitions," Tebas said in a statement posted to social media. "China is and will continue to be a strategic partner for LaLiga." Other major organisations that have incurred the wrath of Beijing and Chinese netizens include fashion brand Dolce & Gabbana, Swiss watchmaker Swatch and the National Basketball Association. Some recovered quickly while others took years. CHINA STATE TV HALTS BROADCASTS Brands including dairy companies Mengniu (2319.HK) and Shanghai Milkground Food Tech (600882.SS) as well as Eastroc Beverage (605499.SS) said they were ceasing all cooperation with Mbappe effective immediately. The companies said they "firmly oppose and have zero tolerance for any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people." China's state television has halted broadcasts of all matches and events involving LaLiga and Mbappe, and all advertisements involving Mbappe have been removed, state-backed media outlet the Paper reported on Tuesday. "Mbappe's team knew, or should have known, what the true cost of Chinese brand endorsements was all about," said Terrence Burns, sports sponsorship expert and CEO of the T. Burns Sports Group. Swiss-based On Holding, which [USN:L4N45A12B TEXT:"signed Mbappe"] in September after he had spent two decades at US rival Nike, welcomed his apology and said it had "deep respect" for China. Accor did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Denmark's Lego, which has a Mbappe building set on sale in China, said it could not comment. The Mbappe set still featured on Lego's Chinese website on Tuesday. 'WHAT DID HE SAY?' Chinese state media outlet China Daily said Mbappe's remark had "triggered a backlash among his Chinese fans, threatened his lucrative commercial relationships and offered a sharp reminder of the limits of celebrity influence". "What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it," the state-backed Global Times added. "The message from Chinese consumers is clear: Respect is not optional; one doesn't get to profit from China while disrespecting it. Not a chance." On Chinese social media platform Weibo, one user wrote about the apology; "Not accepted. Not forgiven!!". State broadcaster CCTV struck a more conciliatory tone, however, saying it would listen to what Mbappe had to say after his apology, and "even more importantly" watch what he does. "We hope La Liga, Real Madrid, and Mbappe himself will genuinely learn a lesson from this, offer a sincere apology, and thoroughly correct their mistakes," CCTV said in a statement. Real Madrid declined to comment. Tebas issued an apology earlier on Tuesday on X and said his organisation deeply regretted the alleged comments that have caused discomfort and offence in China. "We are taking the measures within our reach and working directly with our partners and interlocutors in China to overcome this situation," Tebas wrote. "A relationship built over so many years cannot be damaged by a single episode." TRENDING ON WEIBO As of 0700 GMT, four topics related to Mbappe were still among the top 10 trending searches on Weibo. Some netizens called for China to blacklist Mbappe and reduce his commercial value to zero. These comments received hundreds of likes. Fans have been creating memes superimposing Mbappe's face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to influence decisions at the teams he plays for. Mbappe has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the European press. "In attempting to laugh at himself and his reputation of being a dictator in the locker room, he apparently crossed a red line he didn't know was there," said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. In an interview with L'Equipe last month, Mbappe said that although aspects of the meme trend were harmless fun, the viral ones depicting him as a dictator showed "a lack of political and human awareness". A spokesperson for China's Foreign Ministry said words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people "will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society".

item.title: Privacy group files complaints against Scale AI over alleged worker surveillance
item.description: European digital privacy advocacy group noyb filed five complaints against Scale AI in France, Italy, the Netherlands and Austria on Tuesday, alleging it illegally monitored freelance workers who produce training data for AI models.
item.dc:creator: Leo Marchandon
item.content:encoded: European digital privacy advocacy group noyb filed five complaints against Scale AI in France, Italy, the Netherlands and Austria on Tuesday, alleging it illegally monitored freelance workers who produce training data for AI models. The complaints target Outlier, a platform on which more than 900,000 freelancers perform various tasks that are recorded to create AI training data for clients such as Meta (META.O) , OpenAI and Google (GOOGL.O) . Meta owns 49% of Scale AI. Noyb is asking regulators to fine Scale AI and to examine how the platform assigns tasks. "You don't work when you want," said Thomas Le Bonniec, who spent two years studying the platform for Paris-based research collective DiPLab. "You work when the platform wants you to and there are tasks available." Scale did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The complaints seen by Reuters said up to 19 trackers follow workers while they work, including recording keystrokes and mouse movements every few seconds. An investigation by DiPLab found the resulting file could be rebuilt into a video that replays a work session from start to finish. Workers must also submit ID documents and face video to identity verification firm Persona. The complaints said the checks were invasive, repeated without explanation, and broke EU rules on biometric data. Outlier also uses game-like mechanisms, and bonuses are a key part of its incentive system, DiPLab found. Outlier offered bonuses of $100 to $200 for completing 200 tasks in 24 hours, Le Bonniec said, citing interviews with workers during his investigation. Italy's data protection authority fined delivery platform Glovo in 2021 over similar gamification, he added. Four workers asked Outlier for copies of their data between December 2025 and May 2026. None received an answer, the complaints said.

item.title: Sondeos a boca de urna en Israel apuntan a un punto muerto en elecciones
item.description: Las elecciones en Israel terminaron el martes en un aparente punto muerto, mostraron los sondeos a boca de urna de las principales cadenas de TV, ya que ni el primer ministro Benjamin Netanyahu ni su principal rival, Gadi Eisenkot, parecen estar en camino de obtener la mayoría en la Knesset de 120 escaños.
item.dc:creator: Steven Scheer, Pesha Magid
item.content:encoded: Las elecciones en Israel terminaron el martes en un aparente punto muerto, mostraron los sondeos a boca de urna de las principales cadenas de TV, ya que ni el primer ministro Benjamin Netanyahu ni su principal rival, Gadi Eisenkot, parecen estar en camino de obtener la mayoría en la Knesset de 120 escaños. Este punto muerto podría favorecer a Netanyahu, ya que permitiría al veterano primer ministro permanecer en el poder en funciones mientras los partidos intentan formar una coalición de gobierno. Los resultados definitivos podrían tardar días en conocerse, y el fragmentado sistema político israelí convierte a los partidos más pequeños en posibles "hacedores de reyes". Ningún partido ha conseguido jamás por sí solo 61 escaños en la Knesset, que cuenta con 120 puestos, por lo que las coaliciones son la norma. La votación registró una participación récord, con los israelíes emitiendo su veredicto en tiempos de guerra sobre Netanyahu en las primeras elecciones celebradas desde los ataques liderados por Hamás del 7 de octubre de 2023 y las guerras subsiguientes en Gaza, el Líbano e Irán. El actual líder de la oposición, Yair Lapid, dijo en un comunicado: "Que nadie los confunda: el bloque de Netanyahu ha sufrido una derrota aplastante. Es un colapso total y el público les ha dicho que se vayan a casa". SIN MAYORÍA Las principales cadenas mostraron al bloque liderado por Eisenkot obteniendo entre 52 y 53 escaños, y al bloque liderado por Netanyahu ganando alrededor de 50 escaños. Los 17 a 18 puestos restantes fueron asignados a partidos árabes no alineados en las encuestas a boca de urna. Algunos medios israelíes, incluido el Canal 14, favorable a Netanyahu, proyectaron un resultado mucho más favorable para el primer ministro y sus partidos, afirmando que obtendrían colectivamente 60 escaños. Las políticas de la coalición de derecha de Netanyahu han sido motivo de división a nivel nacional y han agravado el aislamiento internacional de Israel, pero él ha defendido su trayectoria como el único líder con la entereza necesaria para hacer frente a los enemigos de Israel. Netanyahu, de 77 años, ha ocupado el cargo de primer ministro durante casi 19 de los últimos 30 años y ha sobrevivido en repetidas ocasiones a crisis políticas. Se presentó a las elecciones enfrentándose a acusaciones de corrupción de larga data, que él niega, y a críticas por los fallos de los servicios de inteligencia que permitieron a los militantes de Hamás matar a 1.200 personas y tomar 251 rehenes. Eisenkot, exjefe del Estado Mayor y partidario de una línea dura en materia de seguridad de 66 años que perdió a un hijo y a dos sobrinos en la guerra de Gaza, se erigió como el rival más fuerte de Netanyahu, haciendo hincapié en su trayectoria en materia de seguridad al tiempo que se posicionaba como centrista en el ámbito nacional. Entró en política hace solo cuatro años y se unió al gabinete de guerra de Netanyahu tras el ataque de Hamás, pero dimitió ocho meses después, criticando el liderazgo del primer ministro. A menos que uno de ellos consiga reunir una mayoría, Israel se enfrenta a unas prolongadas negociaciones para formar coalición o a nuevas elecciones. "Creo que estas elecciones son las más importantes de todas las que he vivido", afirmó Ruth Epstein, una votante de 81 años de Ramat Gan, cerca de Tel Aviv, que desde hace mucho tiempo vota a la izquierda y que ha votado a los Demócratas, de la oposición. "Me da mucho miedo lo que va a pasar aquí". Louis Lipsky, de Jerusalén y partidario de Netanyahu, dijo que votaba para que el primer ministro se mantuviera en el poder, y le atribuyó el mérito de haber normalizado las relaciones con varios Estados árabes en el marco de los Acuerdos de Abraham de 2020. Netanyahu ha basado su campaña en su liderazgo en las guerras y en el respaldo del presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, su aliado en la guerra contra Irán, quien ha afirmado que deben "terminar el trabajo". Eisenkot dice que la respuesta de Israel —una guerra que, según las autoridades sanitarias, se cobró la vida de más de 74.000 palestinos— fue un fracaso porque Hamás sigue al mando. Reiteró su compromiso de desmantelar o destruir el poder militar y de gobierno de Hamás en Gaza en un plazo de 18 meses tras la formación del Gobierno. Eisenkot ha descartado aliarse con partidos árabes, alegando una falta de valores comunes, aunque algunos expertos prevén que estos puedan respaldar un Gobierno en minoría para garantizar la destitución de Netanyahu.

item.title: Seoul shantytown fire extinguished, Yonhap reports
item.description: A fire that broke out on Tuesday in Guryong village, a shantytown in Seoul's upmarket Gangnam district, affecting 77 households and 107 people, has been extinguished, South Korea's Yonhap news agency said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A fire that broke out on Tuesday in Guryong village, a shantytown in Seoul's upmarket Gangnam district, affecting 77 households and 107 people, has been extinguished, South Korea's Yonhap news agency said. Firefighters extinguished the fire after nearly 13 hours, with one woman suffering a minor leg injury, it added. Yonhap said people had evacuated to an emergency shelter. The National Fire Agency deployed 232 personnel and 110 pieces of equipment to fight the blaze, which began at about 3:50 p.m. local time (0650 GMT) in a temporary structure, Yonhap said. It sent six helicopters to stop the fire from spreading to a nearby mountain. Guryong, often described as Seoul's largest remaining shantytown, emerged in the 1970s and 1980s when families displaced by public works projects settled on the edge of Gangnam without permits. Its densely packed homes are built with flammable materials such as vinyl sheets and plywood. A [USN:L1N3YH00Q TEXT:"major fire"] in the village in January forced hundreds of residents to evacuate.

item.title: King Charles says Commonwealth to confront slavery's injustices, as calls for reparations grow
item.description: King Charles on Tuesday acknowledged the injustices of slavery, saying Commonwealth leaders would discuss the issue at their summit next week, against the backdrop of increasingly vocal demands from the Caribbean that Britain pays reparations for its role in the slave trade.
item.dc:creator: Michael Holden, Isabel Infantes
item.content:encoded: King Charles on Tuesday acknowledged the injustices of slavery, saying Commonwealth leaders would discuss the issue at their summit next week, against the backdrop of increasingly vocal demands from the Caribbean that Britain [USN:L1N44Z0C8 TEXT:"pays reparations"] for its role in the [USN:L1N45O0OI TEXT:"slave trade"]. Speaking in the Bahamas at the start of a Caribbean tour, Charles said it was "only right" to acknowledge "the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond". His remarks come before the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda next week, where Caribbean leaders are expected to press demands for reparations for slavery and colonialism. Charles added that some of what was "best" in Bahamian culture today — "the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright" — was "born out of darkness". Charles and Queen Camilla are visiting the Bahamas and Guyana before travelling to Antigua and Barbuda for the biennial summit of the 56-nation Commonwealth, most of whose members are former British colonies. The issue of reparations has gathered momentum across the Caribbean in recent years. Last month, CARICOM, the regional bloc, said it wanted the matter on the agenda at the summit. "The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice," CARICOM Secretary-General Carla Barnett said last month. Buckingham Palace has indicated that the king would address the issue during the tour, but not [USN:L1N45O0OI TEXT:"offer a formal apology"], in line with British government policy, which also rules out financial reparations. A palace spokesperson said the visit would focus mainly on "modern partnerships and opportunities for the future" in the region, but added that for Charles it was also part of "a lifelong" effort to engage with and educate about "the most shameful aspects of our past". Campaigners and some Caribbean leaders have called on Britain to go further, including through an apology, reparations in the form of financial compensation and the return of cultural artefacts. From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, making it one of the biggest slave-trading nations.

item.title: Israël/Législatives-Participation record, Netanyahu et Eisenkot au coude-à-coude
item.description: Le Premier ministre sortant Benjamin Netanyahu était donné mardi au coude-à-coude avec son rival Gadi Eisenkot, selon les premières estimations, à l'occasion des élections législatives en Israël, premier scrutin national depuis le choc des attaques meurtrières du Hamas le 7 octobre 2023.
item.dc:creator: Steven Scheer, Pesha Magid
item.content:encoded: Le Premier ministre sortant Benjamin Netanyahu était donné mardi au coude-à-coude avec son rival Gadi Eisenkot, selon les premières estimations, à l'occasion des [USN:L6N46C0PJ TEXT:"élections législatives"] en Israël, premier scrutin national depuis le choc des attaques meurtrières du Hamas le 7 octobre 2023. Aucun parti ne bénéficierait de la majorité, la coalition d'opposition menée par l'ancien chef d'état-major de l'armée israélienne [USN:L8N4690LP TEXT:"Gadi Eisenkot"] remporterait 52 sièges à la Knesset, contre 50 pour le Likoud de Benjamin Netanyahu, selon les derniers sondages en sortie d'urne des chaînes de télévision. Les partis arabes non-alignés s'empareraient de 18 sièges. D'autres médias, dont la chaîne de télévision Channel 14 favorable au Premier ministre israélien, rapportent que la coalition de Benjamin Netanyahu pourrait empocher près de 60 sièges. Pour être représentée au Parlement, une liste doit recueillir au moins 3,25% des voix, ce qui lui permet d'obtenir quatre sièges. Aucun parti n'a jamais réussi à emporter seul la majorité absolue (61 sièges) et les gouvernements sont donc le fruit de coalitions, parfois fragiles. Le score serré du scrutin pourrait jouer en faveur de Benjamin Netanyahu qui pourrait s'accrocher au pouvoir à titre intérimaire si aucun parti ne parvenait à former une coalition gouvernementale. Les résultats définitifs de l'élection sont attendus d'ici au 30 octobre et seront officiellement annoncés le 4 novembre. Le chef de l'opposition israélienne Yair Lapid a déclaré que le Likoud avait subi une "défaite cuisante". "C'est une chute totale et la population leur a signifié de rentrer chez eux." Selon la Commission électorale, la participation s'est élevée à 77,7%, un record depuis les élections de 1988 et environ 7 points de plus que lors des dernières élections législatives de 2022. La Commission a évoqué tout au long de la journée des taux précoces de participation "records", alors que de longues files se sont formées devant les bureaux de vote, qui ont ouvert à 07h00 heure locale (05h00 GMT) et ont fermé à 22h00. Vivement critiqué pour n'avoir pu empêcher l'attaque du 7-Octobre, qui a fait plus de 1.200 morts en Israël et conduit l'Etat hébreu à déclencher des guerres à Gaza, au Liban et en Iran, Benjamin Netanyahu, 77 ans, aborde le scrutin affaibli, malgré le soutien affiché du président américain Donald Trump. Ce test électoral a de fait valeur de référendum après le traumatisme du 7-octobre, mais "Bibi", poursuivi par ailleurs pour des faits de corruption, ambitionne de maintenir son record de longévité au pouvoir après 19 années de mandat cumulées (1996-1999, 2009-2021, depuis 2022). Il doit compter avec la concurrence inattendue de l'ancien chef d'état-major de l'armée israélienne [USN:L8N4690LP TEXT:"Gadi Eisenkot"], 66 ans, qui a promis de diligenter une commission d'enquête publique sur les failles présumées de l'appareil sécuritaire israélien le 7 octobre 2023. Dans un message adressé à ses partisans plus de cinq heures après l'ouverture des bureaux de vote, Benjamin Netanyahou a exhorté les Israéliens à voter, affirmant que le taux de participation était élevé chez ses adversaires. "Il faut que le nôtre soit élevé lui aussi. Vous devez tous vous rendre en masse aux urnes", a-t-il déclaré. "C'est un moment décisif." L'INCONNUE EISENKOT Durant la campagne, [USN:L8N46017Y TEXT:"Benjamin Netanyahu"], qui réfute toute responsabilité dans l'échec sécuritaire du 7-Octobre, s'est posé en garant de la sécurité d'Israël malgré son isolement sur la scène internationale et s'est prévalu du soutien exclusif de Donald Trump face à la "menace existentielle" de l'Iran, pays contre lequel il entend "finir le travail". "Je pense que ces élections sont les plus importantes de toutes celles que j’ai connues", témoigne Ruth Epstein, une électrice de gauche de 81 ans résidant à Ramat Gan, près de Tel-Aviv. "J’ai vraiment peur de ce qui va se passer ici." Gadi Eisenkot, qui a perdu son fils de 25 ans et deux neveux dans le conflit dans la bande de Gaza, a accusé Benjamin Netanyahu de "s'appuyer sur une campagne fondée sur la politique de la peur, les mensonges et les menaces", et s'est dit convaincu que Donald Trump travaillerait "en totale coopération avec quelque dirigeant choisi par le peuple". "Je suis convaincu qu’à la fin de la journée, nous assisterons à un changement — un nouvel élan pour l’État d’Israël — qui servira de réparation pour ces trois dernières années et pour cette terrible journée", a déclaré l'ancien officier lors d’une visite au kibboutz Nir Oz dans le sud d’Israël, cible des attaques du 7-Octobre. Il a voté au côté de Gadi Mozes, l’un des 251 otages enlevés alors par le Hamas. À l’instar de Benjamin Netanyahu et de la quasi-totalité des partis juifs, Gadi Eisenkot s’oppose à la création d'un Etat palestinien. Il s'est toutefois montré critique envers les violences commises par les colons juifs à l’encontre des Palestiniens en Cisjordanie occupée, lesquelles sont en recrudescence depuis 2023. MOBILISATION SANS PRÉCÉDENT DE LA MINORITÉ ARABE Les électeurs issus de la minorité arabe d'Israël — israéliens de nationalité mais palestiniens d'origine — se mobilisent en un nombre "sans précédent", a affirmé le candidat palestinien Ahmed Tibi. Ces électeurs, qui représentent environ 21% de la population israélienne, ont traditionnellement un taux de participation électorale inférieur à celui des Israéliens juifs. Gadi Eisenkot a exclu tout partenariat avec les partis arabes, invoquant un manque de valeurs communes. Certains experts estiment toutefois que ceux-ci soutiendraient son gouvernement afin de garantir le départ de Benjamin Netanyahu. Ce dernier a qualifié à plusieurs reprises les électeurs arabo-israéliens de menace, utilisant des termes que ses adversaires jugent racistes. Des voitures arborant les drapeaux du Likoud ont sillonné les rues de Jérusalem mardi, équipées de haut-parleurs diffusant à plein volume l'appel islamique à la prière et proclamant: "Sortez de chez vous tout de suite. Les Arabes votent." Les électeurs sont appelés à renouveler les 120 membres de la Knesset - l'unique chambre du Parlement israélien - pour un mandat de quatre ans, selon un mode de scrutin proportionnel par liste. Le système électoral israélien accorde une grande importance aux petits partis, souvent indispensables à la formation d'une coalition viable. Les Premiers ministres sont ainsi régulièrement contraints de satisfaire leurs exigences pour garantir la survie de leur cabinet. Ainsi Benjamin Netanyahu, qui pourrait de nouveau tirer parti de cette fragmentation politique, mais reste tributaire de l'appui des figures de l'extrême droite [USN:L8N46613P TEXT:"Itamar Ben-Gvir"], qui a voté dans une colonie cisjordanienne de Kiryat Arba, et Bezalel Smotrich, cibles de sanctions de la part de certains pays occidentaux.

item.title: Stocks rise ahead of tech earnings, Fed decision
item.description: MSCI's global equities gauge rose on Tuesday as investors awaited earnings from US technology companies and the Federal Reserve's next policy decision.
item.dc:creator: Sinead Carew, Johann Cherian
item.content:encoded: MSCI's global equities gauge rose on Tuesday as investors awaited earnings from [USN:L3N46A020 TEXT:"US technology companies"] and the Federal Reserve's next policy decision. [USN:L2N46D00J TEXT:"Oil futures"] settled down nearly $2 as investors turned to the prospect of Middle East peace talks, although prices remained near multimonth highs due to shipping disruptions. Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei [USN:L2N46D0FZ TEXT:"met"] Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Tuesday, a day after holding talks with representatives of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. State media said Khamenei had stressed the importance of pursuing Iran's interests and maintaining its conditions for ending the war. A series of AI-related funding announcements on Monday from Meta (META.O) , SpaceX (SPCX.O) and Broadcom (AVGO.O) encouraged investors, along with [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"Anthropic's"] unveiling of its initial public offering filing. "The AI news gave headway to the bulls and got the bond market settled. That's been helping and we've seen small caps perform better," said Sahak Manuelian, managing director for global equities sales and trading at Wedbush Securities. "There seems to be more noise around coming up with some kind of solution to the conflict in the Middle East. Who knows what that means but, having said that, crude oil is trading down and that's a tailwind for stocks," said Manuelian. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 15.99 points, or 0.03%, to 52,377.57, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 45.83 points, or 0.60%, to 7,722.60 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) rose 308.43 points, or 1.18%, to 26,477.81. The Russell 2000 small-cap index (.RUT) finished up 1.2% for its second straight daily advance. Investors were awaiting earnings reports due this week from AI hyperscalers Microsoft (MSFT.O) , Amazon (AMZN.O) and Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , looking for signs their spending is yielding returns as expected. Big Tech earnings could also influence investor appetites for the [USN:L6N46C148 TEXT:"Anthropic"] IPO and Meta's $95 billion equity fundraising. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) rose 6.58 points, or 0.59%, to 1,129.74. Earlier, the pan-European STOXX 600 (.STOXX) index finished up 0.47%. CENTRAL BANKS EXPECTED TO STAY ON HOLD Fed [USN:L6N46518P TEXT:"policymakers"] have indicated they will not raise short-term borrowing costs again on Wednesday, but with inflation concerns front and center, investors think a pause in rate hikes will not last long. Traders are pricing in an increase from the Fed in December. Along with the [USN:L6N46518P TEXT:"Fed"], the European Central Bank and the [USN:L3N46C02N TEXT:"Bank of Japan"] are due to make policy decisions this week, with economists expecting all three to stand pat on interest rates, leaving investors to focus on comments from policymakers to gauge the rates outlook. In [USN:L2N46D0G8 TEXT:"currencies"], the dollar nudged higher against the euro, Japanese yen and sterling as traders prepared for the central bank meetings. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.35% to 102.38, with the euro down 0.43% at $1.1124. Against the Japanese yen , the dollar strengthened 0.28% to 157.94. In [USN:L6N46D13Y TEXT:"fixed income"], US Treasury yields mostly edged higher with investors weighing the outlook for interest rate hikes ahead of Wednesday's Fed decision. The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes rose 1.28 basis points to 4.999% while the 30-year bond yield rose 1.25 basis points to 5.3135%. The 2-year note yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Fed, rose 2.8 basis points to 4.739%. US crude settled down 1.83%, or $1.86, to $99.90 a barrel and Brent finished at $113.88 per barrel, down 1.67%, or $1.93. In [USN:L2N46D0ZD TEXT:"precious metals"], spot gold rose 1.09% to $4,060.29 an ounce, while spot silver rose 0.95% to $54.44 an ounce.

item.title: Israeli exit polls show deadlock, point to setback for Netanyahu
item.description: Israel's wartime election was deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, with Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc running neck and neck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp, leaving neither side with a clear path to power.
item.dc:creator: Maayan Lubell, Lili Bayer, Tamar Beeri
item.content:encoded: Israel's wartime election was deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, with Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc running neck and neck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp, leaving neither side with a clear path to power. The projections pointed to a setback for Netanyahu's coalition, though the deadlock could allow Israel's longest-serving prime minister to remain in power as caretaker during coalition negotiations. "The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu's service as Israel's prime minister ... a worthy leader would have accepted the people's non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics," Eisenkot told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv. Turnout was 77.7%, Israel's Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in 2022. Kan 11 and Channel 13 showed the two blocs level, while Channel 12 gave Eisenkot a narrow edge over Netanyahu's Likud-led camp. None gave either side the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Far-right religious parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were projected to take a combined 13 seats within Netanyahu's bloc. Arab parties outside the two main blocs could hold the balance of power. But Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party and a former military chief, has all but ruled out forming a government with them, complicating his path to power. Final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers. It was the first election since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, called the exit polls a major defeat for Netanyahu's coalition but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner and much could change as votes were counted. NETANYAHU SETBACK, NO CLEAR WINNER Opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement: “Don’t let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home.” Eisenkot, 66, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu's strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically. He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu's war cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticising the prime minister's leadership. [USN:L6N46303T TEXT:"Eisenkot offers a break"] with Netanyahu's leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hardline approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled. Eisenkot says Israel's response — a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities — was a failure because Hamas remains in charge. The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released, on a historic night for turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel. “We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” said Faten Gattas, a candidate in the Joint List, in a speech at the alliance’s headquarters in Nazareth. Candidates hoped high Arab turnout would allow them to play a decisive role in blocking Netanyahu's coalition from returning to power. A WARTIME VERDICT Voters grappled with the trauma of Israel's deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran that followed. While Netanyahu was criticised for the country's biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by killing top leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and deepened Israel's international isolation, but he has portrayed himself as the leader with the mettle to face down Israel's foes.
